question: The rapper Skrilla said of the drill song behind this meme that he never put an actual meaning on it and would not want to. The song was first released in December 2024 and officially released on 7 February 2025, and the meme spread through basketball edits featuring LaMelo Ball. The Overtime Elite player Taylen Kinney amplified it and launched a line of branded canned water. In a YouTube video by Cam Wilder posted on 31 March 2025, Maverick Trevillian became known as the kid behind it after yelling it while making an upward hand gesture. For 10 points, give this two-digit number, chosen by Dictionary.com as its 2025 Word of the Year despite having no real meaning.
answer: 67 [or six seven or 6-7 or six-seven or 6 7 or sixty-seven or sixty seven]

question: Its creator, an Indonesian TikTok user known as Noxa, made it on 28 February 2025 by asking DALL-E for a wake-up drum with a face and legs. It is an anthropomorphic kentongan, a traditional slit drum, and it carries either a wooden drumstick or a baseball bat. It became popular within Italian brainrot, a style of absurdist AI-generated content favoured by younger generations. It appeared in the Roblox game Steal a Brainrot, and its creator's legal team claimed copyright in it despite its AI origin. For 10 points, name this character, whose name pairs an onomatopoeia for its drum with the Indonesian term for the pre-dawn meal eaten during Ramadan.
answer: tung tung tung sahur [or tung tung sahur or tung sahur; prompt on "sahur"]

question: Its first episode, uploaded on 7 February 2023, ran for only 11 seconds. It is made in Source Filmmaker, using assets from Half-Life 2 and Counter-Strike: Source, by Alexey Gerasimov, who is known as Blugray and whose channel was formerly called DaFuq!?Boom! Its plot is a war between singing human-headed fixtures and an alliance of Cameramen, Speakermen and TV Men. Its videos had over 65 billion YouTube views by November 2023, and in July 2024 Michael Bay and Adam Goodman announced film and television adaptations. For 10 points, name this Generation Alpha animated series, whose title pairs a nonsense word with a bathroom fixture.

Early recorded uses include the 2003 Defari track For The Love, Gucci Mane's 2014 track On The Way and J. Cole's 2018 song Brackets. It comes from African American Vernacular English, where it originally conveyed respect for someone slightly older and more experienced. Its current meme sense took off in June 2021, when the TikTok user @callmechosen85 posted a video of a younger person greeting him with it, captioned as if he had officially reached a status. It is now used, often teasingly, for a man who seems older than his age, for example one who struggles with modern slang or grunts when sitting down. For 10 points, give this three-letter clipped form of a word for a parent's brother.

In the 2010s this term was used on forums such as Lookism.net, one of the so-called PSL forums, and it spread to TikTok in the early 2020s. It is associated with looksmaxxing, whose practices include mewing, a tongue-positioning technique, and pursuing hunter eyes and a defined jawline. The Kick livestreamer Clavicular, whose real name is Braden Peters, has been linked to promoting extreme forms of that practice. The framework built around it is widely criticised for promoting harassment. For 10 points, give this verb, a clipped form of an acronym for alpha male of the group, meaning to outshine someone in looks.
answer: mog [or mogging or mogged or mogs or to mog; prompt on "AMOG"]

question: According to the linguist John McWhorter, this word evolved from a common curse, and it has roots in Black Southern, Jamaican and wider African diaspora communities. The streamer YourRAGE said in a video that he always said it instead of the full curse, and that his chat began typing it in 2020 to mock him. The Twitch streamer Kai Cenat helped popularise it, and a TikTok video of 2 October 2023 featuring Fortnite characters was described by The New York Times as a key moment in its spread. The American Dialect Society nominated it for its 2023 Word of the Year. For 10 points, give this Twitch-born exclamation, a respelling of goddamn, that became a Generation Alpha meme.
answer: gyatt [or gyat or gyaat or gyattt; prompt on "gyat damn" or "gyatt damn"]

question: Its foundational idea, the Tropic Premise, was developed in the late 1950s by the British orthodontist John Mew, who argued that crooked teeth come mainly from poor tongue posture rather than genetics. Mew's son Mike brought the technique to YouTube in the 2010s, where an online following coined its name in his honor. It calls for pressing the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth to supposedly reshape the jaw and sharpen the profile over time, a claim no professional orthodontic body endorses. In November 2024, after a seven-year investigation that included a six-year-old patient who suffered seizure-like episodes, Mike Mew was struck off the UK's General Dental Council register. The practice is a staple of looksmaxxing communities alongside pursuing a defined jawline and so-called hunter eyes. For 10 points, name this pseudo-orthodontic tongue-posture technique named for its father-and-son promoters.

The double-x spelling in this term's suffix, later applied to everything from bulkmaxxing to sleepmaxxing, actually originated with this practice in 2010s incel forums, unlike the older single-x min-maxing from tabletop game theory. Its most dangerous fringe technique, bonesmashing, has people strike their own jaw and cheekbones with blunt objects on the mistaken belief that the trauma will make facial bones grow back sharper. Other adherents pursue surgical routes such as jaw contouring and leg-lengthening, or gentler steps like skincare and grooming. The Child Mind Institute has published guidance for parents after the trend spread from fringe forums to mainstream Gen Z apps such as TikTok in the early 2020s. It sits under a wider set of manosphere self-improvement practices that also include mewing and chasing a defined jawline. For 10 points, name this online obsession with maximizing one's physical attractiveness.

This entertainer's birth name is Felix Arvid Ulf Kjellberg, and he registered his channel in 2010 to post Let's Play videos of horror and action games. In 2017 he lost a partnership with Disney's Maker Studios after an antisemitic joke in one of his videos drew widespread criticism. His channel became YouTube's most-subscribed in August 2013 and held that title until being overtaken in April 2019 by the Indian label T-Series, a rivalry marked by his diss track Bitch Lasagna. He calls his fanbase the Bro Army and popularized the catchphrase Smash that like button. For 10 points, name this Swedish YouTuber, for years the platform's most-subscribed creator before being passed by T-Series and later by MrBeast.
answer: PewDiePie [or Felix Kjellberg or Felix Arvid Ulf Kjellberg; prompt on "Felix"]

question: Quality Control Music artists including Migos, Skippa Da Flippa, Rich The Kid and Peewee Longway are credited with creating this dance in Atlanta's hip-hop scene around 2013, and Migos say they debuted it while performing their song Emmitt Smith that November. It spread nationally in 2015 through a Migos single named after it and through Carolina Panthers quarterback Cam Newton's touchdown celebrations, one of which he later declared officially over. It is performed by dropping the head, raising one arm, and tucking the face into the crook of the other, bent arm, resembling a muffled sneeze. For 10 points, name this dance craze whose name is also used for a small hit of concentrated cannabis.

On 1 February 2002, the website WhatReallyHappened published one of the first pieces to summarize this claim, titled "The 9/11 Hijackings – An Inside Job?" Radio host Alex Jones began preaching it within weeks of the September 11 attacks, a stance that cost him more than seventy of his hundred-plus radio station affiliates. The low-budget 2005 documentary Loose Change pushed the claim to a much wider online audience, and the following year saw the founding of the group Architects & Engineers for 9/11 Truth. Its core assertion is that the U.S. government itself orchestrated the September 11 attacks as a false-flag operation, a claim overwhelmingly rejected by the engineering and intelligence communities. It has since become internet shorthand for any far-fetched conspiracy claim, often paired sarcastically with its sister catchphrase about jet fuel and steel beams. For 10 points, give this six-word slogan of the 9/11 Truth movement.
answer: 9/11 was an inside job [or 911 was an inside job]

question: The 2005 documentary Loose Change first popularized this claim as an argument that the World Trade Center towers must have come down by controlled demolition rather than the impact and fires from the planes that struck them. On 8 November 2014, the Redditor Sir-SmokesALot turned it into an absurdist non sequitur by editing it into a "Things a Pony Would Say" webcomic, having a cartoon horse blurt it out at random. The joke format spread through communities such as r/BlackPeopleTwitter and edited Winnie the Pooh comics in early 2015, and it is often abbreviated to a five-letter initialism. It is now used as a stock ironic non sequitur to derail a conversation with an unrelated claim from 9/11 conspiracy theories. For 10 points, give this nine-word truther catchphrase about a type of aircraft fuel and structural steel.

This app launched internationally in September 2017; in its original Chinese market it operates as a separate app called Douyin. Its parent company, ByteDance, merged it in August 2018 with Musical.ly, a lip-sync app it had bought for nearly a billion dollars the previous November, folding that app's mostly American teenage userbase into it. India banned it in 2020 alongside dozens of other Chinese apps amid a border clash with China. In April 2024, the U.S. president signed a law forcing its Chinese owner to divest it or face a ban in the country, and it became the first app to reach ten billion dollars in in-app spending. For 10 points, name this short-form video app known for its algorithmic For You feed.

Its original cooperative zombie-survival mode entered early access on 25 July 2017, developed by Epic Games. Inspired by the runaway success of PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds earlier that year, the studio built a hundred-player last-player-standing mode for it in about two months and released it free-to-play on 26 September 2017. That mode reached ten million players within its first two weeks and 125 million by June 2018. Players swing a pickaxe to harvest materials and build structures for cover, a mechanic that set it apart from its battle royale rivals. For 10 points, name this Epic Games title whose Battle Royale mode became a global pop-culture phenomenon.

In this video game's lore, the tech company Vindertech, founded by the character Vinderman, is credited with minting this currency, whose name is short for VinderTech Bucks. It buys only cosmetic items such as outfits, pickaxes, emotes and wraps that grant no competitive advantage, alongside battle passes. Under the game's original pricing scheme, buying 1,000 of them for real money has cost around ten US dollars, though a 2019 subscription service began granting players a monthly allotment on top of purchases. For 10 points, give this two-word, V-prefixed premium currency of the game Fortnite.

Sixteen-year-old Russell Horning, known as the Backpack Kid, performed this dance move on Saturday Night Live alongside Katy Perry in May 2017, catapulting it to viral fame. It involves swinging both arms front-to-back in unison on one side of the body while the hips swivel the opposite way. Epic Games added it as a purchasable emote in Fortnite's Season 2 Battle Pass that December, prompting Horning to sue the company in 2018 for using the move without his permission or compensation. That suit, along with four others filed against Epic over dance emotes, was withdrawn in 2019 after a Supreme Court copyright ruling required registering a work before suing over it. For 10 points, name this dance craze, also called the floss.

This entertainer was born Darren Jason Watkins Jr. on 21 January 2005 in Cincinnati, Ohio, and created his YouTube channel in 2016 to post gaming content. His livestreams of games like NBA 2K in December 2017 drew as few as two viewers at a time, but in 2021 clips of his energetic, often screaming reactions went viral on TikTok, earning him a million new subscribers within days. He soon became known for supporting the footballer Cristiano Ronaldo and, in 2022, signed to Warner Records to release the single "World Cup." He has since built a following for chaotic in-real-life streams filmed around the world. For 10 points, name this American YouTuber and streamer known by an energetic pseudonym.
answer: IShowSpeed [or Speed or Darren Watkins or Darren Jason Watkins Jr.; prompt on "Darren"]

question: This term first appeared on Urban Dictionary in 2012, the same year some accounts credit the Chicago rapper Chief Keef with popularizing it after using it on a music-video set. It began as an acronym, its three letters standing for a dismissive three-word phrase pointing out a woman across the room. Its use peaked around 2014 before making a slower comeback on platforms like Twitter and Reddit. Lexicographers now describe it as a widely sexist and disparaging slang word, generally aimed at a woman regarded as sexually promiscuous, even as some have tried to reclaim it. For 10 points, give this four-letter slang term, an acronym now used mostly as a slur against women.

Bronx-raised Twitch streamer Kai Cenat says this term started with him and his friend group, and he popularized it further with a 2022 video on how to get it. Actor Tom Holland helped push it into the mainstream during a June 2023 BuzzFeed interview. Many assume it derives from the middle syllable of a word for magnetic personal charm, though Cenat insists it isn't short for anything. Oxford named it its 2023 Word of the Year after more than 32,000 people, including language experts, weighed in. For 10 points, give this slang term for one's skill at charming or flirting with someone, often used in the phrase "rizz up."

The heavily edited black-and-white photos behind this meme come from a 2011 art project called Sleek'N'Tears by photographer Krista Sudmalis, starring the Russian fitness model Ernest Khalimov. A link to that photo series reached Reddit's bodybuilding forum on 15 October 2017, and the very next day it was reposted to 4chan, where users coined its name. That name combines a metric prefix meaning a billion with existing slang for a supremely confident, attractive man. It typically appears as a stoic, chiseled black-and-white portrait, often contrasted against a scrawny "virgin" counterpart in image macros. For 10 points, give this meme name for an exaggerated, larger-than-life ideal of masculinity.

Lexicographers dispute this term's exact origin: one theory traces it to an earlier British slang word for the willing partner of a dominant older man, dating to the 1920s or 30s, while another connects it to an American snack cake, in a sense recorded since 1963. Oxford Dictionaries instead places its coinage in the 1950s. It describes a slim, youthful-looking gay man with little or no body hair, and is often paired in queer slang with an opposite archetype, the bear. By the 1990s it was firmly part of mainstream queer vocabulary, though some critics call its disputed roots ageist. For 10 points, give this gay slang term for a young, slender man.

The 1998 comedy film Pecker helped popularize this term for an act performed by a stripper on a customer, well before gamers adopted it. Rapid crouching over an enemy's corpse in Quake or Counter-Strike as early as 1999 is sometimes cited as its first appearance in games, but the taunt truly took off with a 2001 shooter whose dead players could keep watching the action for a few seconds after being killed. Performing it means gloating over a defeated opponent by repeatedly crouching on top of their fallen body. It has sparked periodic controversy, with some critics likening the taunt to real-world sexual harassment. For 10 points, name this crouching-over-a-corpse taunt, named after a small bag of tea leaves.

This term grew out of "newbie," military slang used by American troops in the Vietnam War for a green recruit fresh to a unit. That older word jumped into early internet culture through the Usenet newsgroup talk.bizarre, with the earliest archived post using it dated 31 May 1988. As l33t-speak spread through 1990s programmer and gamer chatrooms, this shortened, deliberately misspelled offshoot broke off, often written with a zero in place of one of its vowels. Unlike a mere newbie, whose cluelessness is excused by inexperience, this one carries a harsher implication of persistent, incorrigible incompetence. The Concise Oxford English Dictionary added it in 2011. For 10 points, give this gaming slang term for an inexperienced or inept player.

The unrelated root of this term comes from an Old French word for the cuckoo bird, chosen because that species lays its eggs in another bird's nest. Partridge's Dictionary of Slang traces a shortened form of the word to fetish pornography, where by 2000 it had become a genre tag online. A harsher sense meaning "weakling" or "race traitor" emerged on 4chan in 2014 and quickly spread to Reddit. In August 2015 a hashtag combining it with a word for a mainstream conservative peaked during the Republican primary debates, and white nationalists have since used both the hashtag and its shortened form to attack Republican politicians deemed insufficiently hardline. For 10 points, give this pejorative slang term, shortened from a word for a man whose wife is unfaithful.

Far-right writer Theodore Robert Beale, who blogs under the pen name Vox Day, coined this term for a masculinity archetype on a nationalist blog in 2010, describing an introverted, aloof "lone wolf" as an alternative to a more extroverted dominant-male type. It borrows the eighteenth letter of the Greek alphabet as a label within a pseudoscientific hierarchy of male archetypes. On 25 January 2021, a tweet mocking a set of infographics using the term went viral, drawing over 25,000 retweets as most replies mocked the framework. It is now used mostly ironically online, often for a man who thinks he's being edgy and tough while looking anything but. For 10 points, give this Greek letter used as slang for a supposedly self-sufficient loner archetype of masculinity.

On TikTok in March 2024, the user lawfreeza posted a clip captioned "is this rizz" of two Instagram voice messages, the second of which uttered this phrase in response to being called corny. It riffs on Stewie Griffin's Family Guy catchphrase "Erm, what the deuce," swapping in a word already popularized by an unrelated masculinity-archetype meme. Viewers likened the voice's cadence to Squidward from SpongeBob SquarePants, and on 1 April 2024 the TikToker huugh_mungus dubbed the audio over a SpongeBob and Squidward clip, racking up over a million views within two days as a multi-screen "overstimulation" edit. It now functions as a catch-all expression of absurd, exaggerated confusion within so-called brainrot internet humor. For 10 points, give this three-word catchphrase of comic bewilderment that borrows the Greek letter also used for a lone-wolf masculinity archetype.
answer: what the sigma [or erm what the sigma; prompt on sigma]

question: This clipped form of a longer adjective functioned as English police jargon by the 1930s, tracing back further to Britain's 1824 "sus law," a stop-and-search statute that let officers arrest people on mere suspicion and whose discriminatory enforcement helped spark the 1981 Brixton riot. Black internet communities used the short form on forums years before Urban Dictionary's first entry for it appeared in August 2003, and Tyler, the Creator devoted a sketch to it on his show Loiter Squad in 2012. Its use exploded in August 2020 alongside a certain social deduction game's second wave of popularity, becoming the go-to word to call out a fellow crewmate. For 10 points, give this three-letter clipping of "suspicious," popularized among players of Among Us.

Oxford named this term its 2024 Word of the Year after its usage frequency rose 230 percent in a single year, following a public vote of more than 37,000 people. Oxford traces its first recorded use to Henry David Thoreau's 1854 book Walden, though its current sense describes a perceived decline in mental sharpness from consuming excessive trivial online content. It is closely associated with a broader vocabulary of nonsense internet slang popular with Generation Z and Generation Alpha, including terms like "Skibidi" and "Ohio." A subgenre of surreal AI-generated animal characters produced largely in Italy is often labeled with this term as a modifier. For 10 points, give this two-word term for supposed mental decline caused by too much low-quality online content.

The character behind this meme first appeared in a February 2017 YouTube review of Sonic Lost World by Gregzilla, who intentionally warped Knuckles the Echidna's design into a grotesque, googly-eyed figure. Fans of the Twitch streamer Forsen gave the character its national identifier, and its catchphrases, including asking "do you know de way," were lifted from the 2010 Ugandan action film Who Killed Captain Alex? A downloadable model of the character reached VRChat in September 2017, and a January 2018 video by YouTuber Jameskii turned it into a full-blown viral craze there. Its creator later expressed regret over the meme, which critics have condemned as a mockery of African accents. For 10 points, name this VRChat meme, a warped version of a Sonic the Hedgehog character given a fictional Ugandan identity.

This character debuted on Instagram on 15 June 2018, styled by his creators as a stylish traveler posing at real-world tourist spots such as Scotland's Doune Castle and the Isle of Skye. He is a CGI figure combining a realistic human male body with a detailed pig's head and snout, occupying the uncanny valley. On 21 March 2023, the TikTok user rover.joe overlaid one of his selfies with a fake incoming call screen and ringtone, and the resulting videos, captioned with a question asking whether you'll pick up, went viral within days. Users have since made horror, comedic and other remixes of the format. For 10 points, name this anthropomorphic pig-headed internet character, whose calls warrant an urgent decision.

Born in New York City in December 2001 to a Haitian father and Trinidadian mother, this streamer dropped out of SUNY Morrisville in 2020 to focus on content creation. He was recruited into the YouTube collective AMP by fellow Bronx creator Fanum after posting his first video in January 2018. He moved to Twitch in February 2021, and a month-long subathon in February 2023 made him the platform's most-subscribed streamer, a title he lost briefly to Ironmouse in September 2024 before reclaiming it the next month during his Mafiathon event. He is credited with popularizing internet slang terms including Rizz and Fanum tax. For 10 points, name this Twitch streamer known for chaotic collaborative content with his AMP collective.

This former kickboxer rose to notoriety as a social media personality after a brief 2016 stint on the British reality show Big Brother ended when a video surfaced of him hitting a woman, which producers said was consensual and which he denied any wrongdoing over. He was banned from Twitter in 2017 after writing that women bore some responsibility for being sexually assaulted, and he later built an online course called Hustler's University. On 29 December 2022, he was detained in Romania along with his brother Tristan on charges including human trafficking and rape, which he denies, and he was later ordered extradited to the United Kingdom to face separate charges there. For 10 points, name this British-American internet personality known for espousing hypermasculine and misogynistic views.
answer: Andrew Tate [or Emory Andrew Tate III; prompt on "Tate"]

question: This African American Vernacular English term is thought to derive from the phrase "crash dummy" and is often traced to rappers from Baton Rouge, Louisiana, including NBA YoungBoy. On December 18, 2023, the TikTok user @peezyante posted a video defining it that racked up over 1.7 million plays within three months. Used as a verb, it describes someone losing control and, often out of a feeling that they have nothing left to lose, deliberately jeopardizing their own body, relationships or future in a reckless outburst. People who do this habitually are given a noun form of the same two words, and the behavior is often compared online to a "meltdown". The term spread across TikTok in early 2024 and now appears constantly in captions about unhinged, self-destructive behavior after a breakup or provocation. For 10 points, give this two-word slang phrase for a reckless emotional or violent outburst, as in "he is about to ___".

This slang term combines "aura," internet shorthand for a person's charisma or presence, with a gaming term for repeatedly grinding to accumulate a resource. TikTok user h.chua_212 posted an early example of the phrase in January 2024, captioning a video of friends bowling. It exploded into a worldwide phenomenon in mid-2024 after a clip spread of an eleven-year-old Indonesian boy, Rayyan Arkan Dikha, calmly swaying atop the bow of a traditional racing boat during Riau's Pacu Jalur festival while his teammates paddled below him. His unbothered poise was hailed online as the ultimate example of the practice, and imitators worldwide have restaged his pose ever since. A related 2026 trend called "aura battles" saw participants competing head-to-head through posing, mogging and dancing to see who could accumulate the most of this quality. For 10 points, name this slang term for accumulating charisma points through a deliberately cool-looking repeated action, popularized by a dancing Indonesian boat boy.

According to Merriam-Webster, this word has carried the sense of "done for" or "finished" since the nineteenth century, but its current internet usage traces to Australian slang, where it meant ruined, broken or ridiculous before spreading through gaming and hip-hop circles to also mean wasted, dazed or defeated. It doubles as a synonym for "roasted," describing someone who has just been savagely mocked or insulted. Streamers and gamers now use it to describe an unwinnable, hopeless position, often invoking the rhetorical question "chat, am I ___?" to ask an audience whether a situation is truly beyond saving. It can also simply describe exhaustion after a long day or embarrassment after a mistake. For 10 points, give this past-participle slang adjective, food-preparation vocabulary reused online for being finished, doomed or humiliated.

This phrase traces to African American Vernacular English, where the verb "to cap" has meant "to lie," "boast," or "exaggerate" since at least the early twentieth century, feeding into the ritualized insult exchanges known as "capping" that flourished in Black communities by the 1960s. Geto Boys rapper Willie D used a related form, "high cappin'," on a 1989 track, and Atlanta hip-hop artists such as Young Thug and Future later popularized this exact two-word phrase in their own lyrics. Now ubiquitous on TikTok and Twitter, it functions as an assurance that the speaker is being completely honest, while its bare, one-word negation instead accuses someone of lying or exaggerating. For 10 points, give this two-word Gen Z catchphrase, an assurance of sincerity built by negating a slang word for "lie".

Used adverbially since the 1800s to describe something restrained or subdued, this word's modern slang sense of "secretly," "quietly," or "to some extent" is widely credited to African American Vernacular English. It softens whatever statement follows it, letting a speaker admit something mildly embarrassing or understated without fully committing to it, as when confessing to secretly enjoying something uncool. It rose to ubiquity on Twitter, Instagram and Snapchat during the 2010s before becoming one of the most common slang words in English-language memes and captions, often paired with an antonym describing something done openly and intensely. For 10 points, give this hyphenated slang adverb meaning "somewhat" or "secretly," whose opposite is "highkey".

At Axum, this word was used as a royal title as early as the reign of King Ezana around 250 AD, and in pre-1974 Ethiopia it named a rank bestowed on a regional ruler by the Negusa Nagast, or "King of Kings," the title by which Ethiopia's emperors were formally known. On June 2, 2007, twelve-year-old Andrew Lay was asked to spell this word at the Scripps National Spelling Bee; after he requested its language of origin and a definition, a judge explained that "the ___ ruled Ethiopia until the coup of 1974," and the boy's visibly nervous reaction to a word that sounds almost exactly like a well-known racial slur made the clip a long-running internet meme. Some writers have controversially proposed a direct link between this word and that slur, though most linguists instead trace the slur to Latin and Iberian words for "black". For 10 points, give this Ethiopian Semitic title for "king" that a nervous spelling bee contestant once had to define on camera.

In 2013 this animated film's screenplay began circulating across Tumblr and Pastebin as a full-script copypasta, its opening line reading "According to all known laws of aviation, there is no way a bee should be able to fly." Comment sections and chat windows became flooded with its entire dialogue, forcing several platforms to adjust how they displayed walls of unbroken text. Around 2015 and 2016, YouTubers built a whole remix genre around it, including a video by creator AvoidAtAllCosts that plays the film but speeds it up every time a certain insect is mentioned on screen. Its plot follows a recent college graduate named Barry B. Benson, voiced by Jerry Seinfeld, who sues the human race for stealing honey. For 10 points, name this 2007 DreamWorks animated film whose screenplay became a legendary internet copypasta.

On January 14, 2013, an anonymous 4chan poster kicked off a cult internet obsession with this film by posting a rambling greentext story proclaiming its title character to be both "love" and "life." Devotees of that meme, who called themselves "brogres," kept the joke alive online through its peak in late 2014. Loosely based on a 1990 picture book by William Steig, it follows a solitary, onion-loving ogre voiced by Mike Myers who agrees to rescue a princess in order to reclaim his swamp from banished fairy-tale creatures. Its soundtrack's use of Smash Mouth's "All Star" has since become a meme of its own. For 10 points, name this 2001 DreamWorks animated film about a green ogre, subject of the "is love, is life" copypasta.

This rapper, born Daniel Hernandez, built an early online following through his rainbow-colored hair and heavily tattooed face, breaking out with his 2017 single "Gummo." His affiliation with the Nine Trey Gangsta Bloods led to his November 2018 arrest on racketeering and firearms charges, including conspiracy to commit murder. He avoided a lengthy sentence by taking the stand in 2019 and testifying against his own former associates, a move that made him a widely mocked online symbol of "snitching," complete with rat-themed edits and memes. Days after his release from home confinement in May 2020, he dropped the single "Gooba," whose music video briefly set a record for the most views in 24 hours on YouTube. For 10 points, name this rapper and internet punching bag, also known by a number-based nickname derived from his stage name.

This catchphrase was first voiced by British actor Zoe Lister for a television advert released by its airline on December 23, 2022, set to Jess Glynne's song "Hold My Hand." A new version of that ad, uploaded to the airline's YouTube channel in January 2024, showed a family enjoying a carefree package holiday. Starting in March 2025, TikTok users began dubbing Lister's cheerful voiceover over clips of holiday disasters instead, such as sunburns, airport meltdowns and cancelled flights, milking the ironic contrast between the chipper narration and the chaos on screen. The trend went on to soundtrack more than 1.3 million videos, and the airline itself leaned into the joke rather than fight it. For 10 points, give this six-word slogan for a British package-holiday airline, now a byword for vacations gone hilariously wrong.
answer: Nothing beats a Jet2 holiday [or Nothing beats a Jet2holiday; prompt on Jet2]

question: This character is often cited as the biggest breakout hit of a wider genre of surreal AI-generated animal-object hybrids known as Italian brainrot, a genre whose first viral entry, a Nike-wearing shark called Tralalero Tralala, appeared on TikTok in January 2025, followed a month later by a bomb-dropping crocodile hybrid called Bombardiro Crocodilo. Like those characters, it is narrated in an exaggerated, AI-generated Italian-accented voice reciting absurd, rhyming nonsense. Unlike most of its genre-mates, though, its name and design draw on Indonesian rather than Italian culture, referencing a traditional wooden slit drum used to wake a village for a pre-dawn Ramadan meal. For 10 points, name this anthropomorphic drum-on-legs meme character, whose thrice-repeated name imitates the sound of that drum.
answer: tung tung tung sahur [or tung tung sahur or tung sahur; prompt on "sahur"]

question: In November 2025, the companies behind a Roblox game sued the agency Mementum Lab in California's Northern District, seeking a declaratory judgment that the agency holds no U.S. copyright in this character on the grounds that AI-generated works fail copyright law's human-authorship requirement; Mementum countersued for trademark infringement, and a jury trial in that case is scheduled for November 2027. The Roblox game at the center of that suit, Do Big Studios' Steal a Brainrot, had earlier received a cease-and-desist letter over the character and briefly removed it before an unauthorized reintroduction sparked the litigation; that game would go on to peak at over 25 million concurrent players. Its Indonesian creator, an artist billed online only by an alias, has said the design took just fifteen minutes and seven prompts to generate, after an AI image tool badly misread a wooden slit drum called a kentongan as a stick-limbed creature wielding a bat. For 10 points, name this litigated meme character, an Indonesian entry in the Italian brainrot genre whose thrice-repeated name imitates the sound of a drum used to wake villagers for a pre-dawn Ramadan meal.
answer: tung tung tung sahur [or tung tung sahur or tung sahur; prompt on "sahur"]

question: A TikTok theme page known by the handle Home Design began posting absurd, AI-narrated 3D home renovation clips on 4 December 2023, remodeling a child's bedroom in its debut video. The channel belongs to a wider trend of parody remodeling content built around exaggerated running gags. Nearly every one of its videos claims to use this material alongside a companion claim of eco-friendly wood veneers, regardless of what is actually being built. Commentators have linked the joke's mockery of cramped, flimsy spaces to real anxieties over the housing crisis and the rise of micro-apartments. Skits and memes mocking the phrase spread widely across TikTok and Reddit starting in May 2024. For 10 points, name this three-word construction-material catchphrase, naming a zinc-coated, rectangular iron alloy, endlessly repeated in Home Design's parody renovation videos.
answer: galvanised square steel [or galvanized square steel; prompt on galvanized steel or galvanised steel]

question: The word entered English by the 1600s as a noun imitating the sharp, repetitive bark of a small dog, according to the Oxford English Dictionary. Because nonstop human talking reminded people of that kind of barking, a verb sense meaning to talk excessively with little substance developed over time. In mid-2023, TikTok users revived the term as a lighthearted way to mock reaction-video creators and streamers who talk at length. A related noun form has since been reclaimed as a proud badge by people who admit they struggle to stop talking, spawning online communities of self-described holders of that label. For 10 points, give this gerund slang term for talking too much and with little substance, as in "stop ___."

In oculoplastic surgery, this measurement is defined as the angle between the line connecting the eye's inner and outer corners and true horizontal. An upward slant toward the temple, often typical of many East Asian and Mediterranean eye shapes, is nicknamed hunter eyes, while a downward slant toward the cheek is nicknamed prey eyes. Surgeons note it is determined mostly by the bony architecture of the orbital rim and cheekbones rather than by any soft tissue that diet or exercise could change. Surgical correction, called canthopexy or canthoplasty, can shift it by only a few millimeters and carries risks including eyelid malposition and dry eye. Within looksmaxxing communities on TikTok, people with the favorable version of this measurement have mocked those with the unfavorable one, often declaring the situation hopeless with the ironic phrase "it's over." For 10 points, name this angle of the outer eye corner relative to the inner, whose upward or downward slant has become an obsession in online looksmaxxing culture.
answer: canthal tilt [accept positive canthal tilt or negative canthal tilt; prompt on tilt]

question: TikTok user peroxidekaw first applied this nickname to a teenage dancer on 3 April 2024, in a clip comparing his appearance to a distorted image of rapper NBA YoungBoy used to represent an unrelated 2021 meme. Its subject, a teenager later identified as Michael Amato, first appeared in a series of viral clips filmed at a friend's Sweet Sixteen party, alongside another dancer nicknamed Blue Tie Kid. The earlier 2021 meme it echoes began when a TikTok user posted a screenshot of a school computer's login screen bearing a ridiculous two-word name, captioned to mock it. Amato has since joined TikTok under his own account and embraced an abbreviated form of this nickname himself. For 10 points, give this nickname, combining a nationality adjective with the name of an unrelated 2021 shitpost meme, given to a teenage dancer at a viral Sweet Sixteen clip.

On 23 December 2022, YouTuber KC3FEETT uploaded a clip from a Christmas-themed livestream in which a member of the streaming collective AMP kicked down a fellow streamer's door specifically to steal his cookies, a bit that had begun as a spontaneous joke between the two on earlier broadcasts. That AMP member, born Roberto Escanio on 22 August 1997, built a running gag around swiping bites or whole portions of his friends' food on camera. Fellow AMP streamer Kai Cenat's broadcasts were frequent targets of the bit, and clips of it spread widely on YouTube and TikTok through 2023. By late that year, the phrase describing this running gag had become common Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang for taking any portion of someone else's food or belongings without asking, and the phrase was itself later mocked in satirical videos parodying its overuse. For 10 points, give this two-word streamer-slang phrase, formed from an AMP member's stage name plus a word for a government levy, for swiping a share of someone else's food.

Creator Dane Boedigheimer, who posts under the handle DaneBoe, released the debut installment of this web series on 9 October 2009, deliberately timed to fall on his own birthday. The character's design superimposes simple human facial features onto real fruit footage, a low-budget technique Boedigheimer had used in earlier freelance promotional videos. Its title figure torments other produce, including a pear and a marshmallow-like sidekick, with rapid-fire puns until they are abruptly sliced apart off-screen, usually by a knife. The debut video passed a million views within three weeks and more than fifty million within six months, turning Boedigheimer into an early YouTube celebrity. Its success led to a 2012 Cartoon Network television adaptation. For 10 points, name this citrus-themed YouTube character and web series known for its grating catchphrases and gruesome fruit-based deaths.

The earliest known written use of this emoticon appears in a Yu-Gi-Oh! fan-fiction posted on 14 October 2005. Its two identical outer characters represent tightly closed, happy eyes, while the middle letter forms a small cat-like mouth. It spread through anime-focused chatrooms and message boards before becoming closely associated with the furry fandom online. By 2014, it had become an established fixture of Tumblr's internet subculture. Spain's Royal Academy has listed it in its word observatory, defining it simply as an emoticon showing happiness or tenderness. For 10 points, give this three-character emoticon of a cute, closed-eyed face, popular in anime and furry fan communities.

The Oxford English Dictionary traces this term's earliest citation to a 2002 Usenet post, where it originally described drivers deliberately flashing their high beams to provoke other motorists. Its meaning later shifted to online content engineered to be frustrating, provocative or offensive purely to drive up traffic or engagement. Oxford recorded a threefold rise in its usage over the year before naming it a recent Word of the Year. In an online public vote drawing more than 30,000 participants, it beat out several other finalist terms to win that title. For 10 points, give this two-word compound term for content deliberately designed to provoke online anger, Oxford's 2025 Word of the Year.

Born on 27 May 1999 at the Gladys Porter Zoo in Brownsville, Texas, Harambe was a western lowland gorilla transferred to a Midwestern zoo in September 2014. Zoo staff shot him dead on 28 May 2016, one day after his seventeenth birthday, after a three-year-old child climbed into his enclosure and was dragged through its moat. Video of the incident, broadcast by news outlets worldwide, ignited fierce public debate over the zoo's decision and prompted a wave of ironic, melodramatic online tributes to the animal. On 2 July 2016, a Twitter user's post promising to arrive in a state of undress "to avenge" him seeded an early version of what would become this rallying cry. Two days later, comedian Brandon Wardell tweeted its now-standard four-word wording and posted a video of a group of men chanting it, cementing the phrase as one of that year's biggest memes. For 10 points, give this crude four-word rallying cry demanding a certain body part be publicly bared in mock tribute to a gorilla shot dead at the Cincinnati Zoo.
answer: dicks out for Harambe [accept tits out; prompt on Harambe]

question: For years, skeptics on forums and in YouTube investigation videos disputed that a real man was behind this meme's photographs, speculating he was an AI composite or a blend of several different bodybuilders. The Russian model behind them, who has Azerbaijani heritage, eventually broke his silence with a social media post thanking fans for their "kind words" and signing off using the self-deprecating label often paired with this meme in image-macro comparisons. A 2023 melodic techno remix built around this meme's name, produced by g3ox_em and It's Different, became a standard soundtrack for admiring edits and motivational compilations. Its name and stoic black-and-white image were later licensed into a Solana-blockchain cryptocurrency that partnered with a decentralized fitness brand to market itself as a lifestyle token. For 10 points, name this meme, now also a cryptocurrency ticker and techno remix subject, for an exaggerated ideal of stoic, chiseled masculinity.

Early Urban Dictionary entries describing this practice's altered, dissociative mental state date to 2005, though the online community built around it didn't formalize until a dedicated subreddit launched on 23 May 2019. That subreddit is devoted to photos of elaborate, often multi-monitor setups where participants view pornography for extended, deliberately non-climactic edging sessions, and it lent its name to the wider practice's dedicated-room nickname. Starting in late 2022, references to that setup and to themed supply kits for the activity spread more widely online, pushing the underlying term into mainstream meme culture. By the mid-2020s, Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang had stretched the term into a non-sexual sense for being obsessively absorbed in absolutely anything, as in losing hours to a new video game, a celebrity, or even a snack. For 10 points, give this slang term, derived from an old insult for a stupid or dazed person, for prolonged edging toward a state of blank mental dissociation, or, in its watered-down modern sense, for being utterly obsessed with something.

In August 2024, senior community manager John Junyszek publicly denied that this practice was punishable in a numbered entry of a first-person shooter franchise, responding "Yeah, that's not a thing" to a streamer's claim that his squad had been banned for it. Junyszek explained that the timeouts players blamed on the taunt were actually automated penalties for quitting multiple matches in a short span, not moderation targeting the behavior itself. The taunt's name derives from an unrelated real-world sexual act, itself named for the literal kitchen process of dipping a small bag of leaves into hot water. A less common variant performed by female characters or players carries a separate nickname built from crude slang for a different body part. The behavior became a defining feature of Xbox Live culture in the mid-2000s, especially within two Xbox shooter franchises whose multiplayer modes let a dead player's camera linger on their killer. For 10 points, name this crouch-repeating taunt over a defeated opponent, a gaming-culture staple whose ban status one 2024 developer statement had to publicly deny.

On 1 July 2019, this internet personality launched an online store selling merchandise including jars of her own bathwater, priced at thirty dollars each. The next day, she posted an Instagram photo of herself cosplaying Overwatch's D.Va while sitting in a bathtub to promote the product. A viral tweet about the stunt gained over five thousand likes within twenty-four hours, transforming her from a niche Patreon cosplayer into a mainstream punchline and a byword for outrage-driven audience monetization. Her earlier claim to fame came through cosplay photos and videos straddling the line between wholesome gamer-girl aesthetics and adult content. For 10 points, name this British internet personality, or the product named for her fictional gamer-girl persona that she began selling that July.
answer: Gamer Girl Bath Water [or GamerGirl Bath Water; prompt on Belle Delphine]

question: A TikTok posted by creator Ashley Ward on 26 May 2020, urging viewers to think of themselves this way, is widely credited as the spark for this trend's viral spread. Practitioners film cinematic montages of everyday life, gazing wistfully at vast landscapes, dancing alone in the rain, or noticing themselves being noticed in public, scored like a movie soundtrack. Its hashtag has since racked up more than five billion views. Despite sounding self-centered, commentators frame the trend as a form of authentic self-love and self-recognition rather than literal narcissism. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase describing someone who carries themselves as though they were the protagonist of their own life story.

The single letter at the heart of this phrase comes from sports scoreboards and broadcast graphics, where it marks a defeat opposite a letter marking a win. Between 2017 and 2021, that letter combined with a term for earning more replies than an original post to form the "plus ratio" format, a stacked Twitter insult chain often piled on with lines like "you fell off" and "nobody asked." By 2022 that combined format had spread well beyond Twitter into Reddit and YouTube commentary culture. On its own, the phrase can be lobbed at a defeated opponent or used self-deprecatingly to accept one's own setback. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase meaning to accept a defeat, built around a single letter for "loss."

In this 2014 first-person shooter's second mission, protagonist Jack Mitchell attends the funeral of Private Will Irons, who sacrificed himself pushing Mitchell clear of an exploding vehicle. According to level designer Steve Bianchi, the funeral originally had players hammer a pin into the coffin following Navy SEAL rites, a detail scrapped at the last minute after a military advisor objected that the character in question was a Marine, not a SEAL. The replacement quick-time event drew widespread mockery for its forced, oddly literal interactivity at an otherwise solemn memorial scene. For 10 points, give this instruction, delivered onscreen during a mocked Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare funeral scene, now used online both sincerely and sarcastically to acknowledge someone's loss.

Rooted in African American Vernacular English, the verb at the heart of this phrase describes embodying or radiating a particular quality or vibe, as when an outfit is described as doing this for "fall." It sits one notch below a related, more intensely positive term used for someone dressed impressively, which instead describes actively "serving" a look. As the phrase spread widely through influencers, brands and celebrities on social media, commentators noted its AAVE roots were increasingly obscured, sparking broader conversations about linguistic appropriation online. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase, commonly followed by a noun or adjective to describe the vibe or aesthetic something conveys.

This word's emphatic variant, formed by adding a hard "t" sound to its end in the style of African American Vernacular English, is attributed to Southern Black gay slang and the drag and ball community. The earliest known online use of that variant appeared on Twitter in May 2009, though it didn't break into mainstream internet culture until 2018 and 2019 through Black Twitter, TikTok and Instagram. Functioning as a verbal exclamation point, it signals that a speaker's point has been made and no rebuttal is welcome. For 10 points, give this word, borrowed from punctuation terminology, used on its own or with an extra "t" to emphatically end a statement.

Comedian Steven He introduced this exclamation in a 21 September 2021 YouTube skit imagining life on "Asian difficulty mode," where his character's health bar drops to zero the moment an aunty character calls him fat. Three months later, TikToker @liamkearney263 first repurposed a clip of the line to mock pop star Billie Eilish. On 28 December 2021, musician William Lin set a clip of He yelling the phrase to the tune of Bastille's "Pompeii," spreading a gentler, self-deprecating version of the joke. For 10 points, give this two-word exclamation, shouted by Chinese-Irish American comedian Steven He whenever a joke lands an unexpectedly harsh emotional blow.

While promoting Fast & Furious 9 in China, John Cena sat in his car holding a half-melted ice cream cone to his mouth like a microphone and delivered a short promotional monologue entirely in Mandarin. Non-Mandarin-speaking internet users, charmed by his accented pronunciation of the Chinese word for "ice cream," phonetically transcribed what he said into an English-sounding catchphrase that doesn't actually match the word's real tones. For 10 points, give this meme phrase, a garbled English transliteration of John Cena's Mandarin pronunciation of "ice cream."

This abbreviated term first emerged in the early 2010s within K-pop fan communities, describing devotees who held unrealistic beliefs about personal relationships with their favorite idols, with the earliest documented online use dated to 6 April 2014 on the forum OneHallyu. By the early 2020s it had spread far beyond K-pop fandom into general slang for audacious self-confidence or unrealistic optimism, popularized on TikTok through a rhyming phrase pairing it with a nonsense word for "the solution." In March 2025, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used that exact rhyming pairing on the floor of Parliament to mock his political opposition's policies as unrealistic. Cambridge Dictionary formally added the word that August, specifically citing Albanese's parliamentary remark. For 10 points, give this Gen Z slang clipping of "delusional."

Content creator Malaika Norman is credited with the viral audio behind this catchphrase in 2023. On 22 January of that year, TikToker @lmfaomal posted a duet built around it, pairing it with the escalated follow-up line "criminal offensive side eye." Within roughly a month, that duet alone racked up more than 9.6 million plays and 2 million likes, spawning countless reaction-video remixes. For 10 points, give this two-word alliterative-sounding phrase, a hyperbolic descriptor for an exaggerated, disapproving sideways glance.

This creator began his channel on 19 February 2012 under a numbered variant of his current username, since the shorter version was already taken, initially posting Minecraft and Call of Duty gaming content. His January 2017 stunt video, presented as a continuous 24-hour count to 100,000 but actually filmed over roughly 40 hours, helped push him past one million subscribers. He became the most-subscribed individual creator on the platform in November 2022 and its single most-subscribed channel overall by June 2024, later becoming the first individual creator to surpass 500 million subscribers. For 10 points, name this YouTuber, born Jimmy Donaldson, known for elaborate high-budget stunt and giveaway videos.

Know Your Meme traces this phrase's origin to a 2020 Super Smash Bros. tournament, and Urban Dictionary added a formal definition for it on 27 November of that year. Twitch streamers and Roblox players first used it to trash-talk opponents who blamed external factors rather than their own lack of ability for a defeat. It began spreading through memes and reaction GIFs in late 2020, and by 2022 a more sarcastic, meme-ified version had broadened its use to cover almost any real-life mishap, however unrelated to gaming. For 10 points, give this two-word dismissive phrase, telling a complaining gamer that their failure is entirely their own fault.

Borrowed from scoreboards in gaming and sports broadcasts, where a single letter marks a win and another marks a loss, this two-letter prefix system spread into general slang for any successful outcome, good day, or admirable choice. Applied specifically to a term for charisma or flirting skill that Kai Cenat helped popularize into the mainstream, the winning half of that letter pair marks a smooth, confident, well-received attempt at charming someone, as opposed to a clumsy or ignored one earning the opposite letter. Social media compilations of impressively successful pickup attempts, confident one-liners, or charming interactions are frequently captioned with this exact two-word phrase as high praise. For 10 points, give this phrase combining a one-letter mark for victory with a popular slang term for flirting charisma, describing a particularly successful attempt at charm.

Rapper Lil B is credited with using this phrase on social media as far back as 2010, tied to a cooking metaphor for a player on a dominant, creative scoring streak. NBA star James Harden later incorporated a literal stirring-a-pot celebration gesture into his games, amplifying the phrase's association with basketball. Sports commentators and then wider social media adopted it as shorthand for trusting someone's momentum and not interrupting their flow, whether on the court or in an unrelated pursuit like flirting. For 10 points, give this three-word basketball-derived phrase urging bystanders to give a hot-streak performer room to keep doing his thing.
answer: let him cook [or let that boy cook; prompt on cook]

question: A blue baseball-cap emoji now serves as silent digital shorthand for the underlying one-word accusation this phrase denies, typically dropped into a comment to signal disbelief without typing a word. A viral song by the rapper YoungBoy Never Broke Again became a favorite TikTok lip-sync soundtrack that helped push the full two-word phrase to explosive popularity between 2019 and 2020. Merriam-Webster now maintains a dedicated slang-dictionary entry defining the phrase as an assurance of total sincerity. Detractors of the term's spread into mainstream and corporate use have mocked brands and older public figures for using it in cringeworthy, forced ways. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase, an emphatic assurance that the speaker is telling the truth.

An Urban Dictionary entry posted on 3 November 2011 first defined this challenge, in which participants pledge not to reach orgasm for an entire month. It began as a direct parody of a similar month-long challenge built around not shaving, swapping that challenge's public, charitable framing for an entirely private, sexual one. Though conceived as a joke, the challenge exploded across Reddit circlejerk communities, Twitter and YouTube starting in 2017, with some later participants sincerely claiming purported health benefits from abstaining. For 10 points, name this internet challenge, whose title names both a calendar month and slang for achieving orgasm.

The earliest known practitioner of this TikTok Live format is Japanese creator Natuecoco, who began performing idle-animation-style content during her livestreams. In January 2023, a commenter's remark that she resembled a video-game background character inspired streamer Pinkydoll to adopt the same format, repeating a fixed set of phrases and gestures that changed only when viewers sent specific gifts. On 12 July 2023, a viral tweet expressing confusion over one of Pinkydoll's streams helped push the format to mainstream virality that summer. For 10 points, give this term for a TikTok livestreaming style, and the video-game term it borrows for a background character controlled by the game rather than a player.

This one-syllable interjection is generally traced to African American English of the 1980s, itself a shortened form of a much older American expression of confidence and agreement recorded as far back as the 1850s. It circulated for decades within Black American English and hip-hop culture before social media pushed it into mainstream slang during the mid-2010s. Depending on tone, it can express enthusiastic agreement, similar to "for sure," or function as a mocking acceptance of a challenge, similar to "try me." For 10 points, give this slang interjection, homophonous with a noun for a wager, used to affirmatively agree to something.

Derived from a verb meaning to break apart or dramatically surpass expectations, this African American Vernacular English adjective was first used specifically to describe unusually delicious food. Its usage broadened over time to praise anything excellent, not just meals. The word's popularity spiked sharply in March 2021 after catching on among TikTok creators. For 10 points, give this slang adjective, meaning extremely good, often applied to describe a delicious meal.

Meme popularization of this concept began in December 2020 on the Russian imageboard 2ch before spreading to Western social media the following summer. Much of that spread traces to a May 2021 apology video by wrestler John Cena, who bowed to backlash on the Chinese platform Weibo after referring to Taiwan as "the first country" to see a film he was promoting; Western viewers mocked his groveling response by coining a satirical mashup nickname combining his name with that of China's president. The resulting meme format awards or docks large, arbitrary point totals for any action, real or joking, that might please or anger Chinese authorities. In reality, researchers note the actual government system is a fragmented set of databases focused on court-order compliance and business regulation, not the omniscient, universal per-citizen scorecard the meme depicts. For 10 points, name this real Chinese government program, transformed online into a joking shorthand for state approval or punishment.
answer: Chinese Social Credit System [or social credit; accept social credit score]

question: A 2014 photograph of the rapper Drake sitting in the University of Kentucky's locker room in full warm-up gear alongside the actual Wildcats basketball team became the image most associated with this catchphrase nearly a decade later. The exact wording first caught on in late 2021, after a screenshot of an Adidas football Zoom call singled out Manchester United's Scott McTominay among stars like Mohamed Salah and Karim Benzema. On 4 July 2022, a Twitter user paired that older Drake photo with this caption, and as the joke spread globally its distinctly British opening word was increasingly swapped for the more universal "bro." For 10 points, give this mocking catchphrase, aimed at someone in a photo who is obviously not really part of the group they're posing with.
answer: Blud think he on the team [or Who invited my man blud; or Bro thinks he's on the team; prompt on blud]

question: This rapper's own label, Flamboyant Entertainment, released his best-known single, 1998's "Ebonics," a track built entirely around Black American slang terms and their literal definitions. A member of the collective D.I.T.C., or Diggin' in the Crates Crew, he debuted in 1995 with the album Lifestylez ov da Poor & Dangerous. At the time of his death he was in the process of signing to Roc-A-Fella Records as part of a group called The Wolfpack alongside a young Jay-Z. On 15 February 1999, he was shot nine times in the face and chest in a Harlem doorway; a childhood friend was arrested but later released for insufficient evidence, leaving the murder unsolved. For 10 points, give the stage name of this Harlem rapper, born Lamont Coleman.

A short audio clip of someone saying this word in a deflated, disappointed tone first circulated as a Vine before YouTube user Jame Benedict re-uploaded it on 25 March 2016 under a title combining the word itself with "Sound Effect #2." Starting in autumn 2018, the subreddit r/BikiniBottomTwitter popularized pairing that audio with reaction images of a disappointed or exasperated SpongeBob SquarePants, cementing the soundbite as shorthand for a specific kind of cringeworthy, facepalm-inducing situation. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase for a cringeworthy, facepalm-inducing situation, built from a one-syllable interjection derived from "brother" and paired with a certain SpongeBob-associated sound effect.

In an April 2013 home video filmed in Richmond, British Columbia, a young girl points excitedly at a flock of birds and repeatedly misidentifies them using this exclamation, when the birds are actually geese rather than the animal she names. Vine users spread and remixed the clip so widely that it became one of the platform's most nostalgically remembered clips even years after Vine's 2017 shutdown. For 10 points, give this exclamation about misidentified poultry, a beloved early-2010s Vine-era meme.
answer: Look at all those chickens [or Would you look at all those chickens]

question: Former Smosh member Anthony Padilla posted this musical Vine on 30 May 2016, captioned with a rhetorical question asking for the opposite of "gaydar." The clip, celebrating two friends maintaining a conspicuously large gap between them in a jacuzzi, racked up 74,000 likes and 42.8 million loops before Vine's shutdown, and it found a second life on Tumblr, gaining hundreds of thousands of notes within the LGBTQ community, who embraced it as a gentle send-up of straight-male anxiety about physical closeness. It became one of the definitive memes of Pride Month starting in June 2017. For 10 points, give this lengthy Vine-era song title describing two friends relaxing in a jacuzzi while maintaining a very specific, deliberate five-foot distance from each other.
answer: Two bros chilling in a hot tub five feet apart cause they're not gay [or Two bros chillin' in a hot tub; prompt on two bros]

question: Posted on 22 June 2013, the original six-second Vine behind this exchange shows a young boy standing in a dark room, one side of his face lit in blue, with a bright yellow door glowing behind him. Asked a simple addition problem by an off-screen adult, the boy confidently answers with a number that is in fact incorrect by two. That mismatched, unbothered wrong answer's spoken number became a standalone comedic punchline, dropped into countless unrelated Vine skits as the answer to any question at all. For 10 points, give this viral exchange, in which a boy is asked to add two specific numbers and confidently gives the wrong sum.

The earliest known definition of this term, posted to Urban Dictionary in 2008, described an exclamation shouted when someone hit a basketball three-pointer they were confident would go in. Its more famous origin as a dance move traces to February 2014 within Black social media circles, with the earliest video uploaded by Milik Fullilove showing shoulder dips and cycling arm motions. A March 2014 Vine by user Jas Nicole, featuring a dancer nicknamed Lil Meatball, sent the dance itself viral. The word eventually detached from that dance entirely, evolving into a general exclamation for throwing something forcefully or for emphasis on excitement, surprise or frustration. For 10 points, give this Gen Z exclamation and dance move.

This concept traces back to a 30 July 2023 segment on the New Zealand radio show Fletch, Vaughan & Hayley, where hosts helped callers justify questionable purchases with tongue-in-cheek reasoning. On 2 August 2023, TikToker @samjamessssss posted a video pivoting from the earlier "girl dinner" trend to this new one, racking up 3.7 million views within days. By mid-August, TikTok videos built around the concept had collectively been viewed more than 3.3 billion times. For 10 points, give this tongue-in-cheek term for illogical, self-justifying reasoning used to rationalize a purchase, as in the idea that returning an item makes a subsequent purchase effectively free.

TikToker @leahhwoodss is credited with popularizing this rating game in a video posted on 31 May 2022, in which she and her friends passed a camera around a car pitching hypothetical people to rate. Participants start with a baseline score, most often ten out of ten, then reveal one quirky or dealbreaking flaw that might lower it, letting the group re-rate the hypothetical person. Spreading to Twitter the following month, the format collapsed from a group video game into a single-line text template retaining the same basic structure. For 10 points, give this three-word phrasal template, followed by a negative trait that might disqualify an otherwise perfect romantic prospect.

YouTuber Luke TheNotable is widely credited with starting this video format, after his hardcore-mode survival video amassed millions of views and spawned an immediate wave of imitators. He later extended his own version into 200-day and 300-day sequels, while other creators adapted the format to superflat worlds, the Nether, and even playing as a pig instead of Steve. Describing a single world played continuously and narrated after the fact, it became one of the most copied video title templates on YouTube's gaming side. For 10 points, give this video title format, typically followed by a specific in-game milestone reached in the sandbox game Minecraft.
answer: I survived 100 days in Minecraft [or 100 Days in Minecraft; prompt on partial answer]

question: Its author later revealed himself on Reddit in 2013, explaining he wrote the story on a whim after reading two other 'lost episode' creepypastas, 'Suicide Mouse' and 'Dead Bart.' Framed as an account from a Nickelodeon intern, the story describes network staff growing horrified as they review unauthorized, disturbing footage while screening what was supposed to be a season four premiere. First posted to 7chan's paranormal board in April 2010, it's also known by the alternate title 'Red Mist,' after a flash of imagery said to end the segment. For 10 points, name this creepypasta describing a fictional unaired episode in which a SpongeBob SquarePants character takes his own life.

Urban Dictionary's earliest citation for this term dates to April 20th, 2006, though its true origin on 4chan and Usenet imageboards is harder to pin down. Its name plays on how the word sounds when spoken aloud, evoking a type of Italian noodle. The genre spawned countless famous examples, from the aggressive 'Navy Seal' monologue to horror-themed variants that added the prefix 'creepy.' For 10 points, give this term for a block of text repeatedly and often verbatim copied and pasted across internet forums and social media.

Coined around 2007 on 4chan's paranormal board, this genre-defining term describes short, user-generated horror stories and urban legends spread as copied-and-pasted text across the internet. Its most infamous product, a tall, faceless figure in a black suit, was created in 2009 by a Something Awful forums user under the pseudonym Victor Surge, and later inspired a real 2014 stabbing carried out by two children who wanted to 'prove the skeptics wrong.' For 10 points, give this portmanteau term, combining an adjective for unsettling with the word for copied-and-pasted internet text, for the genre of user-generated online horror stories.

The very first entry in this collaborative fiction project, an animate statue that can only move when unobserved, was posted to 4chan's paranormal board in June 2007 using an uncredited photo of a real sculpture by Izumi Kato. Migrating to its own wikidot site by January 2008, the project grew into thousands of numbered entries, each written as a clinical, often redacted document describing a dangerous anomaly. Contributors write in-character as researchers at a secretive organization tasked with securing, containing and studying these anomalies rather than destroying them. For 10 points, give this abbreviation, standing for the fictional foundation's three-word mission, that titles this vast open-source horror and science-fiction wiki.

Created by Becky Sloan and Joseph Pelling, this puppet web series began as a single YouTube short in July 2011 before a crowdfunding campaign expanded it into a six-episode miniseries completed in 2016. Three puppet characters called Red Guy, Yellow Guy and Duck receive lessons on topics like creativity and time from a sinister talking sketchbook and other props that soon turn nightmarish. A television adaptation for adults aired on Britain's Channel 4 in September 2022. For 10 points, give the title of this surreal, unsettling puppet web series and TV series, whose name promises a lack of physical affection alongside fear.

An imageboard called ShrekChan, launched in 2012 as a hub for bizarre content built around a certain green ogre, set the stage for this copypasta's spread the following January. Its content proved so graphic that YouTuber CatalystEXE's narrated animation and, later, Sykotic's full CGI version both became must-see-to-believe viral sensations, with the Fine Brothers' reaction to it in their 'YouTubers React' series exploding past 27 million views in mid-2014. Warned about by content moderators for its disturbing subject matter well before most people had actually read it, the phrase itself became a catchall ironic exclamation of devotion, stripped of its original explicit context. For 10 points, name this infamous 4chan copypasta and internet phrase professing devotion to a certain DreamWorks ogre.

The photo behind this meme was posted to 4chan in July 2012 by an anonymous user claiming to work at the titular fast-food chain, captioned as a warning about what customers were actually eating. Within twenty minutes, other 4chan users had extracted the image's embedded location data, identified the exact restaurant, and alerted local news, getting the poster fired. The meme resurged in 2017 when YouTuber Chills included the story as the fifteenth entry in a video about mysteries 4chan had solved, giving the meme its now-standard numbered title. For 10 points, give this numbered title for a viral photo showing a Burger King employee standing barefoot in a bin of lettuce.
answer: Number 15: Burger King Foot Lettuce [or Burger King Foot Lettuce; prompt on partial answer]

question: Its founder translated the site's original open-source code from Japanese to English using AltaVista's Babel Fish, launching what was meant as an English-language counterpart to the imageboard Futaba Channel. Fifteen-year-old Christopher 'moot' Poole ran the site from its October 2003 launch until stepping down in January 2015, citing the stress of moderating controversies like Gamergate; he sold it later that year to Hiroyuki Nishimura, the founder of the very Japanese site that had inspired it. Famous for anonymous posting and its ever-shifting numbered boards, starting with /b/, it has been credited as the birthplace of countless internet memes and of the hacktivist collective Anonymous. For 10 points, name this anonymous English-language imageboard.

This figure's presence in a Minecraft world is inferred rather than seen directly, through traces like sand pyramids dropped in deserts, two-by-two tunnels bored at right angles, and trees stripped bare of their leaves. Resembling the default player character Steve but with solid white eyes, it was first widely reported in an August 2010 Minecraft Forums thread. Creator Markus 'Notch' Persson confirmed it was a hoax on Twitter, but kept the joke alive by slipping the phrase 'Removed [this entity]' into official patch notes for years afterward. For 10 points, name this urban legend and creepypasta antagonist said to haunt Minecraft worlds.

In the film that originated this term, the choice is offered by Morpheus to Neo: swallow one capsule to remain in comfortable ignorance, or the other to awaken to an uncomfortable truth. Online communities adopted the harsher-sounding capsule's color as an adjective for anyone who claims to have had their eyes opened to some hidden, often unpleasant reality, and the term was later heavily embraced by manosphere, incel and alt-right forums as a badge of ideological awakening. Its popularity spawned variant suffixed slang like 'blackpilled,' for someone who has become nihilistic instead. For 10 points, give this adjective, derived from a Matrix plot device, describing someone newly convinced of a hidden truth, especially in right-wing internet culture.

Originally a 1970s pejorative for a freebase cocaine addict, this term was reclaimed in the mid-2000s by Berkeley rapper Lil B, whose 2007 album with the group The Pack helped popularize its new, positive sense. In a 2010 Complex interview, the rapper defined his version of the word as simply 'being yourself, not being scared of what people think about you.' Internet communities, especially on forums like 4chan, later adopted it as a general term of approval for bold or unapologetic opinions, often paired with another adjective referencing a Matrix-inspired awakening. For 10 points, give this slang adjective, reclaimed from a drug-related insult by rapper Lil B, now used online as praise for someone unapologetically themselves.

This word forms the second half of a rhyming catchphrase whose first half, describing someone as unrealistically deluded, originated in K-pop fan communities to mock fans imagining relationships with idols. Gen Z and Gen Alpha TikTok users adopted the pairing to jokingly suggest that irrational confidence or self-delusion is itself the answer to a problem. Grammatically, it's a playful shortening of a word meaning an answer or resolution. For 10 points, give this word completing the viral catchphrase 'Delulu is the ___,' Gen Alpha internet slang for 'the solution.'

Traditionally describing a lively, zingy flavor reminiscent of citrus peel, this adjective took on a very different meaning around 2022 and 2023 as it spread across TikTok. Videos of men making dramatic, over-the-top gestures began getting tagged with the word, which commentators like teacher Trevor Boffone noted was often a coded way of suggesting someone was gay, queer or feminine. Depending on context, from a playful compliment to a subtler jab, the word's meaning can shift dramatically across TikTok comment sections and meme edits. For 10 points, give this citrus-derived slang adjective, now used online to describe flamboyant behavior, sometimes with a coded implication about someone's sexuality.

This nickname, referencing a retired NFL tight end, belongs to a real youth football player whose parents uploaded a March 2023 video to his own YouTube channel titled "LIVVY DUNNE KNOWS I GOT RIZZ." That clip showed him meeting LSU gymnast Olivia Dunne on campus, and TikToker Henry De Tolla's remix claiming she had "rizzed him up" racked up over 2.3 million views, spawning breathless coverage of their entirely fictional "situationship." Despite viral rumors, he never actually committed to playing for LSU. For 10 points, give this nickname for youth football star Madden San Miguel, borrowed from a hulking Patriots and Buccaneers tight end.

Following the NCAA's 2021 rule change allowing college athletes to profit from their name, image and likeness, this gymnast became one of the most recognizable college athletes in the country, eventually amassing more than 13 million combined followers on TikTok and Instagram. On3 valued her endorsement deals, which include Grubhub, Vuori and American Eagle, at 4.1 million dollars, ranking her the top-earning female college athlete ahead of basketball players Flau'Jae Johnson and Paige Bueckers. She helped her school win its first NCAA women's gymnastics team title in April 2024 before retiring from the sport in April 2025 to focus on modeling. For 10 points, name this LSU gymnast and social media personality, born Olivia Dunne.

This gender-swapped inversion flips a longer-standing phrase believed to have originated on American college campuses in the early 1990s, before hip-hop culture and the 2009 comedy The Hangover helped popularize that original version. Both phrases assert that one type of relationship should take priority over another, with this reversed version urging loyalty to romantic partners instead of friends. For 10 points, give this rhyming phrase, printed on countless novelty T-shirts, that reverses "bros before hoes" to put dating first.

Since beginning human rights work in 2004, this activist has served as Director of Programs at Sexual Minorities Uganda, and has helped organize his country's LGBT pride celebrations despite Uganda's hostile legal climate toward queer people. Global audiences became aware of him after a 2012 Ugandan television interview in which the host opened by demanding an explanation for his sexuality, a clip that went viral online years later in remixed form.
