answer: Wait, That's Illegal [or Wait That's Illegal; or that's illegal]

question: This optimistic reaction comes from Bruce Banner in Avengers: Endgame after an experiment with time travel produces an unintended but useful result. A still of Mark Ruffalo's Professor Hulk paired with the quotation became an image macro in 2019 for a mixed outcome, partial success, or Pyrrhic victory. For 10 points, give this line viewing a result as a total success.
answer: I See This as an Absolute Win [or this is an absolute win; or absolute win]

question: This quotation comes from East View Patriots running back Apollos Hester's interview after a 42–41 comeback win over Vandegrift in 2014. The motivational postgame speech became a reaction format for a statement or story whose ending unexpectedly changes its meaning. For 10 points, give Hester's admission that his team was losing early in the game.
answer: They Had Us in the First Half, Not Gonna Lie [or they had us in the first half; or had us in the first half]

question: This line is said by Frank Reynolds, played by Danny DeVito, while arguing about gun ownership on a local television program in the 2013 It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia episode "Gun Fever Too: Still Hot." A captioned still of the character became a popular reaction image on Facebook and Reddit in 2019. For 10 points, give this transition into Frank's indiscriminate response to two robbers.
answer: So Anyway, I Started Blasting [or Anyway, I Started Blasting; or I Started Blasting]

question: This caption labels pictures and clips of people suddenly becoming energetic, impulsive, or absurdly active late at night. It began with a 2015 Vine by AlliCattt, in which she frantically reports that nearby Domino's locations are closed, and contrasts nighttime behavior with daytime fatigue. For 10 points, give this common caption naming the early-morning hour.
answer: Me at 3AM [or me at 3 am; or me at 3 a.m.]

question: This script-style meme prefix declares that nobody has said or done anything before presenting an unprompted, excessive, or strange action by a person, character, or object. It is commonly followed by a second line intensifying the claim and then a colon naming the unexpected actor. For 10 points, give this first caption line, usually written with a colon.

This emphatic script-style caption usually follows "Nobody:" in memes that set up an unprompted action. By repeating the idea that no person prompted it, it heightens the absurdity of the final line naming a character who acts anyway. For 10 points, give this second caption line, normally written with a colon.

This snowclone caption introduces a group performing an activity, usually an absurd or non sequitur one. It spread through ironic posts in 2019 and became especially associated with a still of the Vulture, Electro, Green Goblin, and Rhino from the 1967 Spider-Man cartoon. For 10 points, give this phrase referring to oneself and one's friends.
answer: Me and the Boys [or me and my boys; or the boys]

question: This shouted command is used as a punchline after someone makes a suspicious, incriminating, or embarrassing online statement. A widely shared 2016 RackaRacka video depicts an exaggerated raid on a party, while later edits use the phrase over abrupt door-breaking footage. For 10 points, give this command attributed to the United States' federal investigative agency.
answer: FBI, Open Up [or FBI Open Up; or FBI open up!]

question: Brad O’Farrell popularized this clip by using its performance to dismiss an unsuccessful person, in the manner of a vaudeville act. Charlie Schmidt originally recorded the footage in 1984, long before uploading the old recording to YouTube in 2007. The performer wears an infant’s blue shirt, which conceals the owner’s hands as he manipulates its front paws. Editors attach this upbeat musical performance to the end of blooper videos, making it seem to play the unfortunate subject offstage. For 10 points, name this musical animal clip featuring an orange feline called Fatso apparently performing a tune on a piano.

Uploaded under the username Gman250, this performance became a Newgrounds sensation before its creator appeared in Weezer’s “Pork and Beans” video. The original upload arrived in December 2004, and its popularity later inspired a contest inviting viewers to make their own versions. Its title borrows repeated Romanian words from the refrain of the recording that accompanies the performer’s exaggerated gestures. Gary Brolsma performs an enthusiastic lip-sync to “Dragostea din tei”, a song by the Moldovan group O-Zone. For 10 points, name this early viral webcam performance in which a seated young man energetically mouths a Romanian pop song.

Its creator explained that this viral composition uses its title as a metaphor for racism against African Americans. A 2007 recording of this song later won the Music category at the YouTube Awards held the following year. The video cuts between its white-shirted performer singing in a studio and shots of him playing a digital piano. A famous on-screen caption explains that the singer moves away from his microphone between phrases so he can breathe. For 10 points, name this Tay Zonday song whose surprisingly deep vocal performance became an early YouTube sensation.

Ryan Etrata and Kevin Flynn created this animation, which circulated on Offtopic before a repost brought it to Newgrounds in 2002. The NBC comedy Ed showed a character watching it in an episode called “The Wedding”, helping it reach television audiences. Its soundtrack is a repetitive novelty recording by the Buckwheat Boyz that later inspired numerous remixes and tribute videos. A Family Guy appearance brought renewed attention to the animation, whose central character is a piece of yellow fruit. For 10 points, name this dancing-banana Flash animation whose title announces the moment for a familiar sandwich filling.

Máni Svavarsson composed this song for an episode called “Robbie’s Dream Team”, featuring the accomplices Bobbie, Tobbie, and Flobbie. Its video features bungled attempts to trap Sportacus, including a large net and slippery banana peels that backfire on the villains. Although it appeared in 2014, the song became especially popular online through comic remixes during the latter part of 2016. Its renewed popularity also supported Stefán Karl Stefánsson, who had been diagnosed with cancer and played the lead singing character. For 10 points, name this LazyTown villain song performed by Robbie Rotten as he teaches his lookalike helpers to catch a superhero.

This track first appeared as the B-side of the “Turbo Love” EP before becoming a separate single and an album track. A widely shared edit of a man diving helped popularize its use as an absurd video soundtrack in early 2017. Katy Perry’s “Swish Swish” video later referenced the editing format that had made this older electronic recording newly recognizable. In that format, a falling person is cut out of the original footage and sent tumbling through an otherworldly background. For 10 points, name this Bag Raiders song used in edits that send people hurtling through space to its synth melody.

Its performer compared the wealthy Seoul area behind this title to Beverly Hills, explaining that his exaggerated persona parodies pretentious behavior. Released in July 2012, this single appeared on the album Psy 6, Part 1 and became a worldwide pop phenomenon. The recording reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped singles charts in countries including Australia and the United Kingdom. In December 2012, its official music video became the first upload on YouTube to reach a billion views. For 10 points, name this internationally viral hit by the South Korean performer PSY, titled after an affluent district of his capital.

Kayode Ewumi plays Reece Simpson, the character whose expression supplies the image for this deliberately faulty form of practical reasoning. The screenshot comes from footage connected with Hood Documentary, a web comedy featured by BBC Three in 2016. One widely circulated caption proposes that refusing to check a bank account prevents its owner from being financially broke. Other captions frame avoiding relationships or ignoring a problem as ingenious solutions, while the pictured character grins at the camera. For 10 points, name this reaction image in which a smiling man taps his temple as if demonstrating a brilliant idea.

One early documented use of this reaction image appeared in a discussion of first-person shooters on an imageboard’s video-game section. Its source is the video for “Hotline Bling”, a 2015 single whose dance moves also generated many other online jokes. Screenshots from that performance spread across music, gaming, fitness, and technology discussions during the following year’s wave of image posts. The distinctive frame shows the performer turning away with a disgusted expression and raising a hand beside his face. For 10 points, name this reaction-image trend featuring a Canadian rapper, commonly used to express rejection or disdain.

An early version of this template ranked “who” against increasingly elaborate variations, including the deliberately extravagant spelling “whomst’d’ve”. Popular examples spread through Reddit in early 2017 before the same structure was applied to subjects such as gaming and politics. The left-hand column lists choices while the images beside them appear increasingly elaborate, suggesting rising levels of intellectual achievement. That apparent ranking is usually ironic: the most ridiculous option receives the most impressive-looking illustration rather than the most sensible choice. For 10 points, name this multi-panel template in which progressively illuminated heads suggest ever greater, often absurd, enlightenment.

This reaction pose became a taunt animation in the gameplay reveal for Nickelodeon All-Star Brawl in 2021. Its original television scene appears in “Little Yellow Book”, in which Squidward reads a diary and learns about a peculiar reaction to plaid. The image spread as a call-and-response format in 2017, repeating another speaker’s statement while deliberately changing its presentation. The pictured yellow character bends forward with his hands behind his back in a pose resembling a chicken. For 10 points, name this cartoon reaction format whose captions alternate uppercase and lowercase letters to ridicule someone else’s words.

Written by Bill Oakley, this television segment later inspired remakes resembling adventure games, music videos, and other radically different visual styles. The original appears within “22 Short Films About Springfield”, where an increasingly frantic host attempts to impress a visiting superintendent. The host passes off fast-food hamburgers as his own cooking and explains their unusual description as an expression used in Albany. He then insists that the glow from a growing kitchen fire is actually a localized appearance of the aurora borealis. For 10 points, name this Simpsons dinner scene turned remix format, featuring Principal Skinner’s increasingly implausible explanations to Superintendent Chalmers.

An early image-macro variation replaced the original method of travel with driving, illustrating an impossible journey using a different verb. The source scene takes place at the Council of Elrond, after the assembled characters discuss destroying a powerful ring. Sean Bean’s character warns that the destination is guarded and dangerous, objecting to the apparent straightforwardness of the proposed mission. Later captions reuse his warning to suggest that an everyday task is much harder than another person assumes. For 10 points, give this familiar cautionary caption from Boromir in Peter Jackson’s first Lord of the Rings film.
answer: One Does Not Simply [or One Does Not Simply Walk into Mordor]

question: Doug Rattmann leaves this warning in hidden areas of a research facility, alerting a later visitor to the deception surrounding its tests. The game’s writers expected an incidental falling hoop to attract attention instead, and were surprised by this message’s online popularity. Players encounter the words repeatedly scrawled on walls away from the normal route through Aperture Science’s carefully controlled chambers. GLaDOS promises Chell a dessert for completing the tests, while the graffiti suggests that the promised reward should never be trusted. For 10 points, give this Portal catchphrase now used for an enticing reward that a person will never actually receive.

The animal in this edit previously appeared at the center of a circular diagram captioned about waking up to yet another occurrence. Its owner identified the original image as a photograph of Ethel, a rescue pet shared in a Facebook group in 2019. The vocal sample came from a Turkish creator’s playful recording, which circulated at different speeds before being paired with the image. Chinese video makers combined that sound with a rotating cutout in 2023, before later versions mixed the effect with pop songs. For 10 points, give the nonsense vocal refrain associated with the rapidly spinning grey feline Ethel in these musical edits.
answer: OIIA OIIA [or Oiiai; or Oo Ee A E A]

question: The original clip used the track “Kak Dela?” before a replacement soundtrack helped it reach a much larger audience. The footage was shared by @fleksa30 in September 2023 and became widely reused in short-video edits during March 2024. An electronic remix of a Raffaella Carrà recording supplies the repetitive Italian vocal that now commonly accompanies the footage. The young animal bobs up and down, raising a paw while the camera framing makes it appear to rotate continuously. For 10 points, name this musical animal video featuring a masked woodland mammal moving around the edge of a round frame.
answer: Pedro Raccoon [or Pedro; or Raccoon Dancing in a Circle]

question: Robert Irwin responded to this hypothetical contest by suggesting that people instead consider how to protect the endangered species involved. A version appeared on Reddit’s r/whowouldwin in 2020, before renewed discussion spread widely across social platforms in April 2025. Commentators disagreed over whether the human side could coordinate effectively enough to overcome an opponent with much greater individual strength. The scenario usually removes weapons from the human participants, making teamwork and willingness to cooperate central points of the argument. For 10 points, name this online debate pitting a century-sized crowd of unarmed humans against a single silverback.
answer: 100 Men vs 1 Gorilla [or 100 Men versus a Gorilla; or One Hundred Men vs One Gorilla; or 100 Men vs a Gorilla; or 100 Men vs Gorilla; or 100 Men versus 1 Gorilla]

question: Roman Originals produced a special charity version in the colors some viewers incorrectly believed they saw in this viral photograph. The photograph originally circulated among people discussing an outfit intended for a wedding on the Scottish island of Colonsay. Caitlin McNeill later reposted the image to Tumblr in February 2015, bringing a local disagreement to a worldwide audience. Researchers investigated the differing perceptions, although the actual garment was blue with black lace rather than white with gold. For 10 points, name this clothing photograph that divided the internet over which of those two pairs of colors it showed.

The original photograph first circulated with a caption about hating sandcastles, an interpretation the subject’s mother disliked because it suggested bullying. Laney Griner uploaded the picture to Flickr in 2007, before its meaning shifted toward celebrating fortunate outcomes and little personal victories. The family later used the image’s fame to promote a fundraising campaign supporting a kidney transplant for the subject’s father. The photograph shows Sammy Griner looking determined while gripping a fistful of sand in a raised hand near his body. For 10 points, name this triumphant baby reaction image, commonly captioned with accounts of things unexpectedly going a person’s way.

Edited versions of this photograph place its young subject beside events such as the sinking of the Titanic or the extinction of dinosaurs. The original scene was a controlled training exercise for firefighters in Mebane, North Carolina, photographed by the subject’s father. A token associated with the photograph was auctioned in 2021, while the family retained the copyright to the underlying image. Four-year-old Zoë Roth looks toward the camera with a knowing smirk, creating the joking impression that she caused the emergency behind her. For 10 points, name this reaction photograph featuring a smiling child in the foreground while a house burns in the background.

The principal rejected this deliberately ridiculous school portrait and required a retake, so the famous image never actually appeared in the yearbook. Kyle Craven bought the sweater vest especially for picture day, intending his exaggerated appearance to amuse his classmates. His friend Ian Davies posted the photograph to Reddit in 2012, using a fictional first name that sounded catchier than the real one. The captions describe embarrassing situations and unfortunate outcomes, often turning an apparently ordinary event into a humiliating personal setback. For 10 points, name this unlucky image-macro character, pictured as a grinning teenager in a sweater vest with visible braces.

This persona originated in a webcam submission for a Justin Bieber sing-off contest promoting a celebrity perfume in 2012. The performer rewrote “Boyfriend” with exaggerated lyrics about monitoring a partner, rather than sincerely describing how she conducted a relationship. A still of Laina Morris from the video became a caption template after the performance attracted attention on YouTube and Reddit. Users paired her intense stare with possessive comments, presenting ordinary romantic behavior as a pretext for surveillance and unreasonable demands. For 10 points, name this wide-eyed reaction-image character, a parody of a romantic partner whose affection becomes excessively clingy and controlling.

The Wii U game Meme Run was removed after a copyright complaint concerning its use of this widely recognized drawing. Carlos Ramirez created the image in Microsoft Paint in 2008 and shared it through his DeviantArt account under the username Whynne. It spread from imageboards into rage comics, becoming a visual stand-in for someone deliberately provoking others for personal amusement. The drawing’s broad, crooked grin conveys smug satisfaction after a prank, and variants often pair it with the brief taunt “Problem?”. For 10 points, name this black-and-white grinning cartoon portrait that became a standard emblem of internet mischief and deliberate provocation.

Jonti Picking explained that the repetitive words in this animation began as placeholder lyrics, but remained in the finished version. The animator, better known as Mr Weebl, released the cartoon online in 2003 using Flash’s ability to repeat indefinitely. A later football variation dressed its woodland performers in England shirts, while another added the sound of vuvuzelas. The original cycles between a group of exercising striped-faced mammals, a mushroom by a tree, and a snake in the desert. For 10 points, name this looping internet cartoon whose chant repeatedly names its principal animals before switching to fungi and a reptile.

Jason Steele originally created this animated short as a birthday gift for their mother, uploading it through the Newgrounds account TypeQueen. Produced by FilmCow, the 2005 short follows a reluctant central character who is persuaded to accompany two brightly colored companions. During the journey, the companions consult a magical Liopleurodon, claiming that its gurgling noises provide directions to their destination. At Candy Mountain, animated letters perform a musical invitation urging the skeptical visitor to enter a cave, which conceals a trap. For 10 points, name this viral cartoon about a weary horned equine lured on an allegedly magical expedition by pink and blue acquaintances.

The underlying Arkady Ostrovsky composition has a title expressing delight at finally returning home, although this famous performance contains no meaningful lyrics. Eduard Khil recorded the television performance in 1976, decades before an upload introduced it to a new international audience. Its online revival gathered momentum in 2010, turning the Russian baritone’s cheerful delivery into an unexpected source of remixes. The familiar internet name imitates the nonsense syllables that Khil sings in place of a conventional verbal narrative. For 10 points, name this viral wordless song performance, remembered for its smiling Soviet-era singer and bouncing stream of syllables.

The musician behind this nickname returned to Eurovision with “Hey, Mamma!” in 2017, when his group finished in third place. His earlier appearance with SunStroke Project during “Run Away” had represented Moldova in the contest’s 2010 edition. Viewers isolated Sergey Stepanov’s instrumental solo from that performance, producing remixes that sometimes repeated it for as long as ten hours. His conspicuous outfit and animated movement helped make the looping passage recognizable independently of the rest of the original song. For 10 points, give this internet nickname for the Moldovan performer whose energetic woodwind solo became an endlessly replayed musical reaction.

The original artist described this character as an animal-like blob, clarifying its unusual body shape after the drawing became popular. StrayRogue posted its original animated GIF in 2018, and DitzyFlama replied with an edit accompanied by music from Super Mario World. The first musical edit used that game’s “Athletic” theme, turning the character’s simple alternating paw movements into a rhythmic performance. Later versions introduced different instruments and songs, and an interactive website allowed visitors to control the illustrated performer themselves. For 10 points, name this white cartoon feline commonly shown tapping a pair of hand drums with its front paws.

Three University of Sheffield students turned this image into a browser game whose clicking totals contribute to a national leaderboard. The original footage showed an animal named Oatmeal chirping at a bug before it was shared online during October 2020. An edited frame exaggerated the animal’s open mouth into a large letter-like oval, contrasting with the photograph of its closed mouth. Musical edits alternate those images in time with a soundtrack, making the animal appear to sing along with the recording. For 10 points, name this wide-mouthed feline reaction image and clicking-game star whose mouth repeatedly switches between closed and O-shaped.

In the original anecdote behind this clip, kitchen pans placed in the sea disappear while the speaker is working at a beach restaurant. Jesús Quintero interviews the storyteller on Ratones Coloraos, a television appearance later repurposed with deliberately inaccurate translations. Some edited versions pretend the interviewee is a technology-company employee openly admitting that a disappointing product was deliberately designed badly. The humor comes from assigning those invented explanations to Juan Joya Borja’s increasingly uncontrollable giggles during the conversation. For 10 points, name this mustached interview subject whose wheezing laughter became a widely reused clip with fake subtitles.

The source recording for this illusion was made by opera singer Jay Aubrey Jones as part of a collection of dictionary pronunciations. A student encountered the ambiguous playback while using Vocabulary.com, and a noisier rerecording helped bring the clip to wider attention. The recording spread across social media in May 2018, with listeners passionately disagreeing about the word spoken by the same voice. Analyses linked the conflicting interpretations to different frequency components, with some listeners focusing on higher sounds and others on lower ones. For 10 points, name this viral audio debate identified by the two different names that listeners heard in one short recording.
answer: "Yanny or Laurel" [or "Laurel or Yanny"; or Yanny Laurel]

question: Rick May voices the character who gives this instruction while the player approaches a group of stationary laser-firing turrets. The command comes from Star Fox 64, the Nintendo sequel released in 1997, and refers to a defensive spacecraft maneuver. Online users later placed the instruction on images and animated GIFs of subjects performing a complete rotation through the air. Google introduced an Easter egg in 2011 that makes the search-results page spin when the phrase is entered. For 10 points, give this four-word command from Peppy Hare, asking the pilot to rotate a spacecraft to evade incoming fire.

Emil Pagliarulo wrote this line while trying to give fantasy guards the personalities of worn-out, semi-retired police officers. The developers intended it as occasional background dialogue, but the game’s systems caused players to hear it much more frequently. Guards in Whiterun use the remark while acknowledging the player’s adventurous activities, presenting themselves as former participants in similar exploits. Its popularity after Skyrim’s 2011 release produced countless variations explaining why a speaker had abandoned an earlier occupation or interest. For 10 points, name the injury in this recurring guard quotation, where a projectile striking a leg joint supposedly ended an adventuring career.
answer: Arrow in the Knee [or Arrow to the Knee; or I Took an Arrow in the Knee]

question: The episode “Attack of the Killer App” supplies this reaction, as a fictional company introduces an eyePhone to enthusiastic customers. During the purchase scene, a cashier warns that the device suffers from poor reception and problems with its battery life. The customer interrupts those objections, waving a handful of dollar bills because his desire for the product outweighs the warnings. Online users repeat the line when an invention or gadget seems so appealing that they want to purchase it immediately. For 10 points, give this eager purchasing demand associated with Fry from Futurama holding out cash toward a seller.

A later episode called “The Girl on the Bus” has the original character send Lisa an animated version of his own reaction. The source scene aired in 1994, when the central father tries to spend the day with the Flanders family. His neighbors decline the invitation, prompting him to withdraw silently into the greenery from which he had appeared. Editors replaced that background with other objects, while the original GIF became a popular way to convey embarrassment and retreat. For 10 points, name this reaction GIF in which a yellow cartoon father gradually disappears into the leaves behind him.
answer: Homer Backs Into Bushes [or Homer Simpson Backs Into Bushes; or Homer Bushes; or Homer Hedge]

question: A widely shared version of this GIF places its central figure in a supermarket toy aisle, apparently unable to locate what he needs. A tutorial later supplied the moving figure against a green background, allowing users to insert him into their own surroundings. The original scene shows Vincent Vega listening while Mia Wallace speaks to him through an intercom in Pulp Fiction. Reused versions place the actor in settings such as an empty classroom, where his searching gestures suggest he has missed some information. For 10 points, name this reaction GIF featuring a suited film character looking around uncertainly after being transplanted into unfamiliar surroundings.

Indian police accounts adapted this sound for road-safety messages, including a warning about how to behave while riding a motorcycle. The recording comes from Teya Dora’s 2023 song “Džanum”, whose original emotional tone emphasizes despair rather than comedy. Its repeated Serbian refrain refers to the singer’s nightmares, although many listeners abroad encountered it without understanding those words. Short-video creators in India and Bangladesh repurposed the clip for comic situations in which something has gone disappointingly wrong. For 10 points, give the repeated phrase used as the popular name for this melancholy Serbian chorus turned comic reaction sound.

The original home-video clip also circulated under the descriptive title “Brick Breaking Experiment Gone Wrong” before its shouted dialogue became better known. America’s Funniest Home Videos shared the footage through its official accounts in February 2016, several years before the sound’s later revival. In the clip, a boy builds a tower of bricks on a glass-topped piece of living-room furniture until the weight makes it collapse. The child’s alarmed reaction became a widely reused lip-sync sound in 2021, appearing in staged mishaps and comic performances. For 10 points, give the panicked exclamation from this viral clip, announcing that the family’s glass furniture has shattered beneath the bricks.
answer: "Oh No! Our Table! It’s Broken!" [or "Our Table! It’s Broken!"]

question: An early appearance of this rage-comic character circulated through a FunnyJunk thread titled “April Fools” in 2010. Later examples moved beyond the original four-panel format into vertical strips, dialogue-heavy comics, and even animated GIFs. The character also became an image-macro template, with captions describing disappointing attempts to connect with other people. Its name expanded into a general expression for feeling permanently excluded from friendship or romance, especially around Valentine’s Day. For 10 points, name this lonely rage-comic character whose two-word caption suggests that the speaker will remain without companionship indefinitely.

The face behind this template was traced from “Naked King”, a chapter of the science-fiction manga Gantz. An early widely shared version on Tumblr complained about an unanswered text message, using abbreviated spelling rather than standard written English. Later versions retained the exasperated face while substituting a different subject and action into the same accusatory sentence structure. The grammar resembles hurried phone messages, and the character’s raised hands reinforce its intense frustration at someone else’s behavior. For 10 points, name this rage-comic figure whose caption reduces a complaint beginning “why do you not” to three short written units.

May Oswald said she promoted this drawing using several accounts and prepared example comics to suggest how others could use it. One of those early examples showed an animal reacting to being petted, illustrating the expression’s association with unusual pleasure. The illustration circulated in 2010 and became part of the rage-comic vocabulary, rather than originating as a photograph of a person. Its caption is a short Spanish expression meaning “I like it”, paired with a face suggesting an odd mixture of discomfort and satisfaction. For 10 points, name this rage face used to convey awkward enjoyment or unexpectedly pleased approval of a strange situation.

Sam Smith created this illustration for a T-shirt sold by Lonely Dinosaur, before online captions gave it an independent comic identity. The artist combined several reference images, adapting an eagle’s talon into a claw and adjusting the eye to create a contemplative expression. Smith said a friend who studied philosophy and hunched thoughtfully over a desk helped inspire the original design. Image macros place paradoxes and metaphysical questions beside the creature, presenting ordinary contradictions as profound subjects for reflection. For 10 points, name this pondering prehistoric predator, whose title blends a thinker’s occupation with the name of a swift dinosaur.

Its source photograph was taken by George Mobley and used to illustrate a National Geographic fact sheet about an Adélie species. The original template’s blue background contrasts with a red version that reverses the image and gives the character much greater confidence. Hybrid versions divide the format between those two personalities, allowing a single encounter to begin well before suddenly becoming embarrassing. Captions usually describe an uncomfortable interaction and a clumsy response, turning familiar conversational mistakes into jokes about personal insecurity. For 10 points, name this image-macro character featuring a flightless Antarctic bird that repeatedly mishandles encounters with other people.

An early caption for this image distorted the words for favorite books, helping establish the spelling convention that later defined the format. The photograph reached Reddit in March 2012, where users turned the subject’s excited expression into a reusable reaction image. The captions imitate the altered pronunciation associated with an orthodontic retainer, replacing normal vowels with exaggerated written sounds. In the original picture, a young reader holds three volumes from the Goosebumps children’s horror series and opens her mouth with excitement. For 10 points, give this deliberately distorted version of “oh my God”, commonly paired with a photograph of an enthusiastic horror-book reader.

This animation began as a demonstration for Character Studio, a software add-on used with Autodesk’s three-dimensional modeling tools. An existing skeleton’s movement was applied to a diapered toddler model, producing a computer-generated performer rather than filmed human footage. Copies circulated through email and CompuServe before animated GIF versions carried the figure to many early personal websites. A popular musical version used Blue Swede’s “Hooked on a Feeling”, and the character also appeared on Ally McBeal. For 10 points, name this early internet animation showing a computer-rendered infant rhythmically moving its body in a looping routine.

Deidre LaCarte created this page during a competition with her sister and a friend to attract the most website visitors. The GeoCities site was named in tribute to her pet, with a deliberate extra letter inserted into the animal’s species name. Its layout repeated four small animated GIFs in rows, while a short audio sample played continuously in the background. That sample sped up Roger Miller’s “Whistle-Stop”, a tune from the opening credits of Disney’s animated Robin Hood. For 10 points, name this early musical website filled with rows of rhythmically moving cartoon rodents and a high-pitched looping tune.

Forrest Whaley used Microsoft Paint to animate this Bryant Oden recording, helping a lyric video become a much larger viral success. The animated version appeared on the forrestfire101 channel in 2009, following an earlier upload by its composer. Its story escalates until an irritated seller threatens to glue his persistent customer to a tree if the repeated requests continue. The seller finally takes the visitor to buy grapes, only for the visitor to express interest in lemonade instead. For 10 points, name this animated musical story about a yellow waterbird repeatedly asking a lemonade-stand operator for grapes.

This 2007 Neil Cicierega video won the Comedy category at the following year’s YouTube Awards after attracting millions of viewers. Its finale reveals that the rhythmic sound driving the performance comes from a concealed explosive device discovered by Ron Weasley. After the explosion, Voldemort performs his own name to the melody of “Lollipop”, replacing the ensemble that had appeared before him. The performance starts when Severus Snape hears a catchy beat and begins repeating his name, soon joined by other Hogwarts characters. For 10 points, name this specific wizard-parody video in which miniature figures chant their names in rhythm to an unexplained repeating sound.
answer: The Mysterious Ticking Noise [or Potter Puppet Pals: The Mysterious Ticking Noise] [prompt on Potter Puppet Pals by asking "Which video?"]

question: The Gregory Brothers transformed this man’s delighted commentary into an Auto-Tuned song shortly after the original recording became widely shared. Jimmy Kimmel helped attract attention to the footage by linking it in July 2010 and later interviewing its creator. Paul “Bear” Vasquez filmed the scene from his property near Yosemite, recording his increasingly emotional reaction to the view. He cries with happiness and repeatedly wonders what the sight means as the camera shows brightly colored arcs across the sky. For 10 points, name this viral nature-reaction video about a pair of nested atmospheric arches, whose observer is overwhelmed by their beauty.

The boys’ father uploaded this home movie because its file was too large to email to their grandfather in the United States. The 56-second clip reached YouTube in May 2007 and became an especially recognizable example of an ordinary family moment going viral. It shows two young English brothers sitting together, with the older child initially treating the younger child’s behavior as a game. The older brother, Harry, reacts more painfully when the infant closes his teeth more firmly, before both children return to smiling. For 10 points, name this famous home video in which a toddler complains that his younger brother has nipped his outstretched hand.

The recording was originally intended to let an absent mother see her son’s experience surrounding the removal of an extra tooth. The family later earned advertising revenue from the viral clip and donated part of its merchandise income to oral-health charities. The central child is still reacting to anesthesia while sitting buckled into a vehicle beside the parent holding the camera. He asks whether the situation is real life and whether the strange feeling will last forever, then briefly rises and screams. For 10 points, name this viral car-seat monologue featuring a disoriented young boy recovering from a visit to have a tooth removed.

The site founded under this title let readers create captioned images using a submission tool called the LOL Builder. Eric Nakagawa and Kari Unebasami started it in 2007, and a later investor group acquired it under the leadership of Ben Huh. Its name came from a caption placed on a photograph of Happycat, rather than from a slogan originally devised for the business. The site helped popularize lolspeak and animal image macros, bringing intentionally unusual grammar to a broad online audience. For 10 points, give this feline’s grammatically mangled request for a burger, which became the title of a major internet-humor website.

This image-macro series exaggerates a television commentator’s favored explanation for structures such as the Egyptian pyramids into a universal answer. Its source program began airing on the History Channel in 2010 and explored speculative claims about visitors from beyond Earth. The screenshot features Giorgio Tsoukalos, whose recognizable appearance became shorthand for the show’s approach to unexplained historical achievements. Captions pose a mystery and then attribute it to extraterrestrials, regardless of whether that explanation has any reasonable connection to the question. For 10 points, name this reaction-image series, sharing its title with a television program about purported otherworldly visitors in the distant past.

The photograph used in this template originally promoted Gridiron Gang, a sports film in which its subject played Malcolm Moore. Its humor draws on the host of Pimp My Ride installing elaborate extras such as fish tanks and fireplaces in participants’ vehicles. Captions build a recursive joke by placing something the recipient enjoys inside another object, enabling the activity to happen within itself. The rapper Xzibit supplies the smiling portrait, and his television persona turns an ordinary upgrade into an absurdly nested customization. For 10 points, give this two-word greeting that begins a familiar image-macro formula about hearing what someone likes and installing more of it.

This template comes from Allie Brosh’s comic “This Is Why I’ll Never Be an Adult”, published on Hyperbole and a Half. The original contrasts a burst of enthusiasm for household responsibilities with the difficulty of maintaining that enthusiasm over time. Users adapted a panel from the comic by changing the intended action and object, making exaggerated commitment into a reusable caption. The character itself is also redrawn as other figures, while the wording still suggests performing an activity with wildly comprehensive determination. For 10 points, name this image-macro formula expressing the desire to clean, collect, or otherwise act on every available item without exception.

Spoofs of this line appeared after a theatrical trailer circulated, before audiences had even seen the full Zack Snyder adaptation. Its source is 300, based on Frank Miller’s graphic novel and presenting a stylized account of conflict with the Persian empire. In the scene, an emissary demands submission to Xerxes, provoking a furious response from King Leonidas and his guards. The king delivers the shouted line immediately before kicking the messenger into a deep well, creating a much-parodied dramatic moment. For 10 points, give the three-word declaration used in edits of Leonidas’s furious kick, asserting the identity of the city he rules.

Later in the same awards ceremony, Beyoncé invited the interrupted recipient back onto the stage to complete her acceptance speech. The incident occurred at Radio City Music Hall during the 2009 MTV Video Music Awards, following the Best Female Video announcement. Taylor Swift had won for a music video when another performer unexpectedly seized her microphone to argue that Beyoncé deserved greater recognition. Image macros subsequently reused the interruption as a formula for abruptly praising something else during another person’s moment of attention. For 10 points, give the colloquial promise supposedly allowing a speaker to continue, made infamous by West’s interruption of Swift.

Comedy Central promoted a new season in 2012 using versions of this caption structure, acknowledging a format viewers had developed online. The original facial expression appears in “The Lesser of Two Evils”, an episode involving the show’s delivery-company employees. A later opening sequence reused the format to wonder whether the viewer was seeing a new installment or a previously watched rerun. Two lines of caption present competing explanations for the same observation, making the pictured character’s narrowed eyes an expression of indecision. For 10 points, name this suspicious squinting cartoon reaction, commonly used to compare two possibilities in a hesitant internal monologue.

The picture behind this character appeared on the cover of Ma Gangsta, an album associated with the rap group Beantown Mafia. Blake Boston later explained that his mother had taken the original photograph, which became widely shared in 2011. The character’s distinctive fitted cap became an independent visual shorthand, pasted onto other people and objects to suggest similar behavior. Captions portray a selfish acquaintance who takes advantage of others, borrowing possessions or enjoying hospitality without offering anything in return. For 10 points, name this freeloading image-macro character, pictured standing in a doorway in baggy clothes and a sideways cap.

An early popular caption for this character describes a houseguest who sleeps on someone’s couch and then prepares breakfast for the host. The template circulated through Canvas in 2011, where users produced hundreds of remixes after the portrait was uploaded. A square-jawed smiling face forms the central photograph, while the text supplies examples of unexpectedly considerate behavior toward other people. The character rewards trust and shows empathy, reversing the familiar image-macro joke about a selfish acquaintance exploiting everyone around him. For 10 points, name this alliteratively named, unusually kind internet character whose captions turn everyday interactions into examples of generosity.

An influential caption sarcastically suggests that a recent graduate must now know everything, establishing the patronizing tone associated with this template. Earlier uses of the same screenshot included the dismissive phrase “You must be new here” before the later caption style became established. The source scene introduces the Everlasting Gobstopper, an experimental sweet shown to children touring an extraordinary factory. Gene Wilder’s expression from a 1971 musical film became a reusable response to people boasting about supposedly impressive knowledge or achievements. For 10 points, name this sarcastic reaction image featuring a famous screen confectioner, usually paired with insincerely impressed responses to another person.

Will King photographed the subject of this image during the 2012 Cooper River Bridge Run in Charleston, South Carolina. After the pictures appeared on Flickr and Facebook, a friend’s comment supplied the label that accompanied the image’s spread to Reddit. Users isolated Zeddie Little’s face from the crowd and placed it in other photographs, amplifying the impression of effortless attractiveness. The original captures him smiling while running, apparently looking ready for a portrait despite participating in an athletic event. For 10 points, name this handsome-runner image whose exaggerated title celebrates someone looking remarkably camera-ready even in the middle of a race.

The original photograph featured a pet named Boba Fett and appeared in a relationship-discussion thread on The Mushroom Kingdom messageboard. The owner placed the animal’s head on a multicolored background, producing the visual template that later acquired two-line captions. Its descendants replaced that head with different creatures and people, giving each new figure a recognizable personality or behavioral stereotype. Typical captions present guidance that is deliberately irresponsible or absurd, creating a comic mismatch with the friendly-looking central portrait. For 10 points, name this early image-macro character showing a smiling puppy on a six-color wheel while offering terrible recommendations.

The source screenshot captures its character while medieval knights are pursuing him, well before the image acquired philosophical captions. A Vulture gallery cataloguing an actor’s facial expressions included the frame, which subsequently circulated as an online reaction image. An early caption wonders whether humans actually can breathe in space and are merely being prevented from discovering that possibility. Later examples retain the startled expression while proposing increasingly implausible explanations for ordinary experiences and supposed hidden truths. For 10 points, name this paranoid image-macro character, pictured as Ted with a frightened expression in Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure.

Will Lyman, known for narrating Frontline, supplies the voice describing the improbable achievements of this fictional advertising character. The campaign featured actor Jonathan Goldsmith as an elegant, bearded adventurer whose supposedly extraordinary experiences established his refined taste. Online captions adapted the contrast between his usual habits and occasional choices, turning the advertising script into a flexible comic formula. The original commercials promote Dos Equis, and the character signs off with the advice “Stay thirsty, my friends”. For 10 points, give the superlative title of this beer-advertising personality, whose image introduces statements about what he does only occasionally.
answer: The Most Interesting Man in the World [or Most Interesting Man]

question: The accessory in this portrait was a Christmas present purchased from the Etsy shop Whisker Kisses for an animal named Emilio. A photograph posted to Something Awful in January 2011 spread to Reddit and image-caption generators within a few days. The resulting template places the formally dressed animal against a starburst background, giving it the appearance of a miniature executive. Captions imitate a workplace supervisor’s requests, but add a feline twist to the expected instructions about office duties and employee behavior. For 10 points, name this image-macro boss, an ordinary household pet whose necktie makes it look ready to manage a company.

An early image using this face pairs it with a bag of carrots whose ingredient list simply identifies the contents as carrots. The outlined illustration was prepared for a rage comic shared on Reddit in 2011, adapting an existing film screenshot. That frame comes from Vampire’s Kiss, where Nicolas Cage plays Peter Loew, a troubled literary agent convinced he is becoming a vampire. The resulting reaction feigns astonishment at an observation that should already have been obvious to everyone involved in the conversation. For 10 points, give this sarcastic three-word expression of surprise, associated online with an exaggerated drawing of Cage’s face.

A related text emoticon represents this character using paired V-shaped claws around a face marked with several small tentacles. One early caption offered the character as a replacement for an existing internet template, suggesting himself when a new example was needed. Later captions ask about an unrelated problem before proposing the same alien as a solution, regardless of the actual situation. The pictured character is a lobster-like doctor whose professional confidence is undermined by his poor knowledge of human anatomy. For 10 points, give this rhetorical suggestion that repeatedly nominates Planet Express’s alien physician as the answer to almost any request.

A GIF contest on Dump.fm helped popularize the animated version of this response, drawing inspiration from an earlier smug-looking canine image. Creators circulated a reusable editing template in 2010, allowing many different pictured subjects to receive the same visual transformation. The animation typically lowers a pair of sunglasses onto the subject’s face, giving the final pose a deliberately unbothered attitude. Its accompanying expression dismisses another person’s objection by insisting that an unwelcome situation must simply be accepted as it stands. For 10 points, give this three-word retort commonly paired with falling sunglasses when someone refuses to apologize or accommodate a complaint.

Barney Stinson uses this expression in “Aldrin Justice”, an episode of How I Met Your Mother that aired in 2006. A later illustrated version appeared in online comics, turning the television catchphrase into a reaction to apparently difficult tasks. The standard figure crosses its arms and wears a smug expression, presenting itself as undaunted by the proposed undertaking. Related versions change the response to consideration or refusal, allowing the same basic comic situation to end with a different decision. For 10 points, give this two-word declaration of willingness to attempt something difficult, commonly paired with a confident rage-comic stick figure.

A Robot Chicken episode parodied the original event in 2005, several years before captioned still images became a popular version of the joke. The source footage comes from a September 2004 television giveaway in which audience members received new Pontiac G6 vehicles. Later image macros substitute other gifts or outcomes, including upvotes or illness, while preserving the host’s exuberant repetition. The format humorously distributes the same object or experience to everyone present, whether that universal distribution is welcome or unfortunate. For 10 points, give the excited announcement associated with Winfrey repeatedly pointing toward audience members during her famous automobile giveaway.
answer: You Get a Car [or Oprah You Get a Car]

question: A tenth-anniversary remix of this recording features Big Freedia, Dorian Electra, and 3OH!3, recasting the original as hyperpop. Clarence Jey and Patrice Wilson wrote and produced the original through ARK Music Factory, with Wilson also contributing an uncredited rap verse. The heavily Auto-Tuned single went viral in 2011, generating widespread criticism, parody performances, and arguments about its deliberately simple lyrics. Its teenage singer describes her morning routine and looks forward to the approaching weekend in the accompanying music video. For 10 points, name this Rebecca Black debut single whose title is the weekday immediately before Saturday.

Its creators intended this promotional recording to be a comically unsuccessful song, but its unexpected popularity instead brought them international attention. The Norwegian brothers behind Ylvis made it to advertise a new season of their television program rather than launch a conventional pop career. Production duo Stargate helped create the polished electronic accompaniment, making an intentionally absurd premise sound like a potential dance hit. The lyrics contrast familiar animal calls with invented nonsense sounds for a woodland creature whose usual vocalization is less widely imitated. For 10 points, name this 2013 novelty hit that asks about the sound made by a bushy-tailed canine.

The unlikely winner of this fictional battle is Fred Rogers, who outlasts the collection of celebrities and characters brought together by the song. Neil Cicierega wrote the recording under the name Lemon Demon, while Shawn Vulliez created the accompanying Flash animation. The collaborators submitted the video to Newgrounds in December 2005, where it won a weekly audience award soon afterward. The premise assembles recognizable figures from popular culture into an enormous brawl, treating absurd crossovers as if they belonged in the same contest. For 10 points, name this animated Lemon Demon battle song, whose emphatic title repeats a word meaning final or unsurpassable.
answer: The Ultimate Showdown of Ultimate Destiny [or The Ultimate Showdown]

question: The performer originally presented a shorter version of this routine in 2003, before the expanded recording became an early YouTube phenomenon. Its soundtrack moves through recordings including “Hound Dog”, “Y.M.C.A.”, and “Thriller”, presenting recognizable musical eras in rapid succession. Judson Laipply uploaded the filmed stage performance in April 2006, and the clip repeatedly held the site’s most-viewed position. The routine follows its changing music with matching physical movements, allowing a single performer to imitate many familiar styles within minutes. For 10 points, name this viral stage medley showing an entertainer moving through decades of popular choreography.

Gary Clarkson and Christian Langdon practiced an early version of this activity in Taunton, before a friend created a Facebook page for it. The later name became associated with Australian participants, and the photo-sharing fad reached a worldwide peak in 2011. The joke depends on adopting the same expressionless pose in an incongruous public location, then sharing a photograph of the result. Participants keep their bodies straight and rigid, with their palms against their sides and their faces directed toward the supporting surface. For 10 points, name this internet posing fad whose name likens the motionless, horizontal participant to a piece of timber.

The soundtrack beneath this irreverent wildlife commentary includes the Prelude from Bach’s sixth suite for solo cello. The narrator, known as Randall, added his own energetic voice to existing National Geographic Wild footage rather than filming new material.
